When constructing a semantic model of a system or when structuring computer code, there are several notions of computation that one might consider. The popular ones can be monads, applicative functors and arrows. Each of these notions of computation has particular characteristics that makes them more suitable for some tasks than for others. In fact, these representations can be unified as monoids in a monodial category, and there is much to be gained from unifying all three different notions under a single conceptual framework.
Monads are known to be monoids in a monoidal category of endofunctors
Arrows have been recently shown to be strong monoids in a monoidal category of profunctors
Applicative functors are usually presented as lax monoidal functors with a compatible strength, or monoids in a monoidal category of endofunctors using the Day convolution as a tensor
For every set M we can construct the monoid of endomorphisms (M\to M, \circ , \text {id}).

M is a sub-monoid of a monoid M' if there is an injection i : M \hookrightarrow M' such that i(e) = e' and i(a \circ b) = i(a) \circ ' i(b) for all a, b \in M. Every monoid M is a sub-monoid of the monoid of endomorphisms (M\to M, \circ , \text {id}).

This can be proved by constructing an injection map \text {rep} : M\to (M\to M) by \text {rep} : a \mapsto \lambda x.a\circ x, which is easy to verify that \text {rep} is a monoid homomorphism. Moreover, \text {rep} is an injection, since we have a function \text {abs} : (M\to M) \to M given by \text {abs} : f \mapsto f(e). and \text {abs}\circ \text {rep} = \text {id}_M.
The Cayley representation can be adapted to the List ([a], ++, []) in Haskell, resulting the famous Difference Lists.

html:pre.html:code:
type EList a = [a] -> [a]
rep :: [a] -> EList a rep xs = (xs ++)
abs :: EList a -> [a] abs f = f []

The ordinary notion of monoid in category Set of sets and functions is restrictive, so generalize monoids to other categories. What we need are notions of
a pairing operation for expressing the type of the multiplication,
a type for expressing the unit.
We can not directly extend set binary functions X \times X \to X to monoid multiplication in a category, because the category may not have products. Instead, we need to use a bifunctor \otimes : C \times C \to C which abstracts the product operation. The unit object is a special object I in the category.
The idea of currying a function can be generalized to a monoidal category with exponential.

Let A be an object of a monoidal category (C, \otimes , \alpha , \lambda , \rho ). An exponential -^A is the right adjoint to the functor - \otimes A, which is characterised by the an isomorphism:
\lfloor -\rfloor : \hom (X \otimes A, B) \cong \hom (X, B^A) : \lceil - \rceil
natural in X and B. The counit of the adjunction is the evaluation map \ev _B : B^A \otimes A \to B. When the exponential to A exists, we say A is an exponent. A monoidal category with all exponentials is called a right-closed monoidal category or said to have exponentials.
For a set A we can generate the free monoid A^*. We can then define the notion of free monoid in terms of monoidal category.

Monoids in a monoidal category C and monoid homomorphisms form a category, denoted by \text {Mon}(C). When the left-adjoint (-)^* to the forgetful functor U : \text {Mon(C)} \to C exists, it maps an object X to the free monoid on X.

It is well known that the free monoid over a set A is the set of lists of A. In Haskell this is just the list type List a.
data List a = Nil | Cons a (List a)
Given a monoid (M, e, m) in C, and a monic i : M' \hookrightarrow M in PC such that for some unique maps e' and m', the following diagram commutes:

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then (M', e', m') is a sub-monoid of (M, e, m), induced by the monic i, which is a monoid monomorphism from M' to M.
Every exponent in a monoidal category induces a monoid of endomorphisms.

Let (C, \otimes , I, \alpha , \lambda , \rho ) be a monoidal category. The monoid of endomorphisms on any exponent A \in C is given by the diagram:
I \xrightarrow {i_A} A^A \xleftarrow {c_A} A^A \otimes A^A
where i_A and c_A are defined:
\begin {align*} i_A &= \lfloor I \otimes A \xrightarrow {\lambda _A} A \rfloor \\ c_A &= \lfloor (A^A \otimes A^A)\otimes A \xrightarrow {\alpha ^{-1}} A^A\otimes (A^A \otimes A) \xrightarrow {\text {id}_{A^A} \otimes \text {ev}_A} A^A\otimes A \xrightarrow {\text {ev}_A} A \rfloor \end {align*}
The Cayley theorem states that every monoid in a monoidal category is a sub-monoid of endomorphisms whenever M is an exponent.

Let \text {End} = ([\text {Set}, \text {Set}], \circ , \text {Id}, \alpha , \lambda , \rho ) be a (strict, i.e. \alpha ,\lambda ,\rho are identities) monoidal category of endofunctors. A monoid in this category consists of
an endofunctor M : \text {Set} \to \text {Set}
a natural transformation \mu : M \circ M \to M
a unit e : \text {Id} \to M such that the following diagrams commute:

\begin {tikzcd} {M\circ M} && {M\circ \text {Id}} \\ \\ {\text {Id}\circ M} && M \arrow ["m", from=1-1, to=3-3] \arrow ["Me", from=1-3, to=1-1] \arrow [equal, from=1-3, to=3-3] \arrow ["eM", from=3-1, to=1-1] \arrow [equal, from=3-1, to=3-3] \end {tikzcd}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A monoid in \text {End} is called a monad. That is where the slogan "a monad is a monoid in the category of endofunctors" comes from.
The monad can be implemented as the type class Triple in Haskell.

The idea to generalize the behavior of functions in mathematics and logic led to the development of the lambda calculus. The lambda calculus is a formal system for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application using variable binding and substitution. In dealing with functions there are two construction principles and one evaluation rule.
Construction Principles: note that expressions do not force to be meaningful.
Function Abstraction: \lambda x.M
Function Application: M N, this only produces a new expression, in which the function has not yet been executed.
Evaluation Rule
Beta Reduction: (\lambda x.M)N\to M[x:=N] The beta reduction makes use of the substitution M[x:=N] which represents the result of replacing all free occurrences of x in M with N. Note that the application is left associative, that is, MNP means (MN)P. And application has the highest precedence, that is, \lambda x.MN means \lambda x.(MN).

The multi-argument function \lambda x_1\ldots x_n.M is defined as \lambda x_1.(\lambda x_2.(\ldots (\lambda x_n.M)\ldots )) (right associative), that is, simulated by a sequence of single-argument functions. The later function is called curried function and the process of transforming a multi-argument function into a sequence of single-argument functions is called currying.
Expressions in the lambda calculus is called terms. The set of terms is denoted \Lambda .

Let \Lambda be the set of lambda terms. Then \Lambda is defined inductively as follows: (V is the set of variables)
Variable: \forall x\in V, x\in \Lambda
Abstraction: \forall x\in V, M\in \Lambda , \lambda x.M\in \Lambda
Application: \forall M,N\in \Lambda , (MN)\in \Lambda
Another way to define \Lambda is to use the following grammar (The 3 possibilities are separated by |): \Lambda = V | \lambda V.\Lambda | \Lambda \Lambda
With the following recursive definition we can determine what the subterms of a give \lambda \text {-term} are. Here we use a concept named multiset.
The definition above uses a notation \equiv which means syntactic equality here.
The substerm mapping satisfies the following lemma.

Variable occurrences in a \lambda \text {-term} can be divided into 3 categories:
Bound Occurrences: x is bound in M if x is the argument of an abstraction in M.
Free Occurrences: x is free in M if x is not bound by any abstraction in M.
Binding Occurrences: something after a lambda notation \lambda We mainly focus on the free variables of a term.
The \lambda \text {-term} M is closed if \text {FV}(M) = \emptyset . A closed \lambda \text {-term} is also called a combinator. The set of all combinators is denoted by \Lambda ^0.

Functions in \lambda \text {-calculus} have the property that the name of the binding variables is irrelevant. In order to describe this equality we need to define a relation called \alpha \text {-conversion} or \alpha \text {-equivalence}, which is based on the process of renaming binding variables.

Let M^{x\to y} be the result of replacing all free occurrences of x in M with y. The relation renaming is expression with the symbol =_\alpha : \lambda x.M=_\alpha \lambda y.M^{x\to y} if y\not \in \text {FV}(M) and y is not a binding variable in M.
The definition of renaming should be extended to more general terms.

The \alpha equivalence is a relation between \lambda \text {-term}, defined as follows:
Renaming: \lambda x. M =_\alpha \lambda y. M^{x\to y} if y\not \in \text {FV}(M) and y is not a binding variable in M.
Compatibility: If M=_\alpha N then \lambda x.M=_\alpha \lambda x.N and ML =_\alpha NL, LM =_\alpha LN.
Reflexivity: M=_\alpha M.
Symmetry: If M=_\alpha N then N=_\alpha M.
Transitivity: If M=_\alpha N and N=_\alpha L then M=_\alpha L.
The first principle is the basis of alpha equivalence, which is the same as renaming. The last 3 properties ensures that =_\alpha is an equivalence relation.
If M=_\alpha N then we say M and N are \alpha \text {-equivalent} or \alpha \text {-convertible}. M is an \alpha \text {-variant} of N and vice versa.
In previous sections we informally mentioned the concept of substitution. Now we give a precise formulation

The substitution is defined by the following rules:
M[x:=N]:\equiv N
y[x:=N]:\equiv y if y\not \equiv x
(PQ)[x:=N]:\equiv (P[x:=N])(Q[x:=N])
(\lambda y.P)[x:=N]:\equiv \lambda z.P^{y\to z}[x:=N] if \lambda z.P^{y\to z} =_\alpha \lambda y.P and z\not \in \text {FV}(N) The terms with form P[x:=N] are not \lambda \text {-term}, but we can regard them as a meta notation that appears in the substitution process and the result contains no such terms.
Renaming can be considered as a special case of substitution. We can show that M^{x\to u}=_\alpha M[x:=u] if the conditions of renaming are satisfied.
We may do sequential substitution in a term, that is, doing a number of substitutions consecutively. And we have the following lemma, which states that the order of substitution is important.
Let x\not \equiv y and assume x\not \in \text {FV}(L). Then L[y:=N][x:=M] \equiv L[x:=M][y:=N[x:=M]].

As we have seen, the relation =_\alpha is an equivalence relation. Hence we can define the set of equivalence classes of terms with respect to =_\alpha . Now we can identify a term with its equivalence class. We still use \equiv for syntactic equality modulo \alpha \text {-equivalence}.
\alpha \text {-equivalence} is a congruence relation, which means that it is conserved by elementary process of term construction.

Let L=_\alpha M and N=_\alpha P.
LN =_\alpha MP
\lambda x.L =_\alpha \lambda x.M
L[x:=N] =_\alpha M[x:=P]

The Barendregt Convention states that we should avoid using the same variable name in different abstractions. This is to avoid the confusion of free variables. It states that we choose the names for the binding variables in a \lambda \text {-term} in such a manner that they are all different, and each of them differs from all free variables occurring in the term.
Since we have formally defined the substitution, we can rephrase the reduction as a relation on \lambda \text {-term}, namely \beta \text {-reduction}.

One step beta reduction (\to _\beta ) is defined as follows:
Basis:
(\lambda x.M)N\to _\beta M[x:=N]
Compatibility: If M\to _\beta N then \lambda x.M\to _\beta \lambda x.N, ML\to _\beta NL and LM\to _\beta LN.
The term of the form (\lambda x.M)N is called a redex (reducible expression). The term of the form M[x:=N] is called the contractum (of the redex).

An interesting example named omega combinator of beta reduction is the following:
((\lambda x.(x\space x))\space (\lambda x.(x\space x))) \to _\beta ((\lambda x.(x\space x))\space (\lambda x.(x\space x)))
The result of the beta reduction is the same term as the original term, and never terminates.
We can often perform a sequence of beta reductions. This leads to the definition.

The (zero-or-more-step) beta reduction (\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta }) is a generalized version of the one step beta reduction. M\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } N if there exists n\geq 0 and there are terms M_0,M_1,\ldots ,M_n such that M_0=M, M_n=N and M_i\to _\beta M_{i+1} for 0\leq i<n. In other words there exists a chain of one-step beta reductions from M to N.
M\equiv M_0\to _\beta M_1\to _\beta \cdots \to _\beta M_n\equiv N

html:ul.html:li: Compatibility: \twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } extends \to _\beta , i.e. if M\to _\beta N then M\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } N.

Transitivity:
M\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } N \land N\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } P \implies M\twoheadrightarrow _{\beta } P

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recently I have been studying some work on Hole, and found some interesting things. As stated in Semantic Foundations for Program Editors, expression hole can be seen as metavariables of contextual modal type theory (CMTT). That is, expression holes can have types and are surrounded by contexts, just as metavariables in CMTT are associated with types and contexts. This note is a brief summary of the paper Contextual Modal Type Theory.

Contextual modal type theory provides an elegant and uniform foundation for understanding metavariables and explicit substitutions. Context is common in logic because the truth of a proposition can depend on the context we consider it in rather than being absolute. Narrowing our scope we may think of a context as consisting of the hypothesis that we made to establish a final conclusion.

There are two main approaches to intuitionistic modal logic.
Nominal: Assign names to contexts and includes explicit judgments to relate them.
Structural: Identifies the context with propositions it contains. In this article we carry this idea further which allows arbitrary contexts to be captured within a proposition.

The philosophical foundation of our development is MLTT approaches of separating judgments and propositions. The most basic judgment is the truth of a proposition, A\space \text {true}. We explain the meaning of a proposition by presenting the means of inferring its truth via introduction rules, and exploiting the knowledge of its truth via elimination rules. In this section we assume there are some atomic proposition P and we define implication A\to B and a contextual modal operator [\Psi ]A where \Psi is a context.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter: If \Gamma \vdash A\space \text {true} and \Gamma ,x:A\space \text {true},\Gamma '\vdash C\space \space \text {true} then \Gamma ,\Gamma '\vdash C\space \text {true}. (Note that this rule is admissible)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A is categorically true or valid if its truth does not depend on any hypotheses about the truth of other propositions. Instead it may depend on the validity of other proposition, because their validity may not depend on truth assumptions.
Conversely if A is valid we can conclude that it is true

In terms of a multiple world semantics, we say that A is valid if A is true in every possible world. We require that A must be true in a world about which we assume nothing (\Gamma = \cdot ), except the constant-true propositions \Delta .
Note that by the definition of validity we can immediately reduce the goal of proving A\space \text {valid} into proving A\space \text {true}, which is captured by the principle of substitution.
If \Delta ;\cdot \vdash A\space \text {true} and (\Delta ,u::A\space \text {valid},\Delta ');\Gamma \vdash C\space \text {true}, then (\Delta ,\Delta ');\Gamma \vdash C\space \text {true}.
With the categorical judgment we can introduce the modal operator for necessary truth \square A.

A\space \text {valid} expresses that A is true in any world. In this section we relativize this judgment: let \Psi = y_1:B_1\space \text {true}, \cdots , y_n:B_n\space \text {true} be a list of assumptions. We say that A is valid relative \Psi (denoted A\space \text {valid}[\Psi ]) if A is true in every world in which B_1,\cdots ,B_n are true. Similarly we generalized assumptions about validity so that \Delta now has the form u_1::A_1\space \text {valid}[\Psi _1], \cdots , u_n::A_n\space \text {valid}[\Psi _n].
As common in PL, we refer to \Psi as a context and to the judgment A\space \text {valid}[\Psi ] as contextual validity.
To prove A\space \text {valid}[\Psi ] we only required to prove A using only \Psi without any hypotheses about the truth:
If \Delta ;\Psi \vdash A\space \text {true} and (\Delta ,u::A\space \text {valid}[\Psi ],\Delta ');\Gamma \vdash C\space \text {true} then (\Delta ,\Delta ');\Gamma \vdash C\space \text {true}.
The precondition implies \Delta ;\Gamma \vdash A\space \text {valid}[\Psi ] and by the substitution principle of hypotheses judgments we can justify this rule.

Set is a common concept in mathematics. This post is a brief introduction to set theory aimed at complete all basic knowledge of set theory. The following topics will be covered
Zermelo-Fraenkel Axioms and Axiom of Choice
Cardinality
Set theory constructions
In this post, we use the Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC).

ZFC is the abbreviation of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice. The axioms of ZFC are listed below.
Axiom of Extensionality: Two sets are equal if and only if they have the same elements.
Axiom of Pairing: For any two sets a and b, there exists a set \{ a,b \} whose elements are exactly a and b.
Axiom schema of Separation: Let P is a property of sets. P(u) means u satisfies the property P. then for any set X exists Y = \{ u \in X | P(u) \}.
Axiom of Union: For any set X (a family of sets), exists union set \bigcup X :\equiv \{ u:\exists v\in X \text { such that } u\in v \}.
Axiom of Power Set: For any set X, exists the power P(X) :\equiv \{ Y:Y\subseteq X \}.
Axiom of Infinity: There exists a set \omega such that \emptyset \in \omega and for any x\in \omega , x\cup \{ x \}\in \omega .
Axiom of Regularity: For any non-empty set there is a minimal element with respect to the membership relation.
Axiom schema of Replacement: Let F be a function where \text {dom } f = X, then for any set X exists a set Y = \{ F(x):x\in X \}.
This function is not the normal function but some logical stuff.
Axiom of Choice: For any family of non-empty sets X, there exists a function f:X\to \bigcup X such that for any x\in X, f(x)\in x.
Let (X_i)_{i\in I} be a family of sets.

html:p.fr:tex: \bigcup _{i\in I}X_i = \set {x:\exists i\in I \text { such that } x\in X_i}

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
\bigcap _{i\in I}X_i = \set {x:\forall i\in I, x\in X_i}
Note that I \neq \emptyset here.

html:p.fr:tex: \prod _{i\in I}X_i = \set {(x_i)_{i\in I}:\forall i\in I, x_i\in X_i}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: And principles of set theory
Two sets are equal if and only if they have the same elements.
Given a set A and a property P(x), there exists a set B such that x\in B \iff x\in A \land P(x).
We then define the Cartesian product of two sets
Given two sets A and B, the Cartesian product A\times B is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b) where a\in A and b\in B.
With the Cartesian product, we can define the relation

A relation R is a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets A and B, i.e. R\subseteq A\times B. If (a,b)\in R, we write aRb.
A relation that between X and itself is called homogeneous relation.

An equivalence relation R on a set A is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Reflexive: \forall x\in A, xRx
Symmetric: \forall x,y\in A, xRy\implies yRx
Transitive: \forall x,y,z\in A, xRy\land yRz\implies xRz We often denote the equivalence relation by \sim .

Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set A. For any element a\in A, the equivalence class of a is the set [a] = \set {b\in A:b\sim a}. The set of all equivalence classes is denoted by A/\sim , which is called the quotient set of A by \sim .
The equivalence class of a is also denoted by \overline {a}.
One of the most important relations is the order relation. The basic order relation is the preorder.

A preorder is a relation \leq that is reflexive and transitive.
Reflexive: a\leq a
Transitive: a\leq b and b\leq c implies a\leq c

A (non-strict) partial order is a relation \leq that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
Reflexive: a\leq a
Antisymmetric: a\leq b and b\leq a implies a=b
Transitive: a\leq b and b\leq c implies a\leq c A non-strict partial order is also known as an antisymmetric preorder.
And the strict partial order (notice the difference between asymmetric and antisymmetric)

A strict partial order is a relation < that is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive.
Irreflexive: \neg (a<a)
Asymmetric: a<b implies \neg (b<a)
Transitive: a<b and b<c implies a<c
With the definition of order, we can define the upper bound and lower bound

Let a subset S of a partially ordered set (P, \leq ), S is bounded above if there exists x \in P such that \forall y \in S, y \leq x. And x is called an upper bound of S. Dually, S is bounded below if there exists x \in P such that \forall y \in S, x \leq y. And x is called a lower bound of S.
An element x\in P is a supremum of S, if for all upper bounds z \in P of S, x \leq z. Denoted as x = \sup S.
An element x\in P is a infimum of S, if for all lower bounds z \in P of S, z \leq x. Denoted as x = \inf S.

Let X and Y be sets then a function f:X \to Y is a mapping that sends each element of X to a unique element of Y, denoted by f(x) = y. Function is a special case of relation, and it is a relation that is left-total and right-unique.
f \in X \times Y \text { and } \forall x \in X, \exists ! y \in Y, (x,y) \in f
X is said to be the domain of f and Y is said to be the codomain of f, where we denote X = \text {dom } f and Y = \text {cod } f.

Two functions f:X\to Y and g:Y\to Z can be composed to form a new function g \circ f : X \to Z, where the composition is defined by
(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))
The set of all functions from X to Y is denoted by \hom _\text {set}(X, Y).
The isomorphism function is defined as follows

Let X and Y be sets and f: X \to Y be a function. The function f is called an isomorphism if it is both injective and surjective. In other words, there exists a function g: Y \to X such that
g \circ f = \text {id}_X \text { and } f \circ g = \text {id}_Y
where \text {id}_X and \text {id}_Y are the identity functions on X and Y respectively. And we say f is invertible and g is the inverse of f. If there is a isomorphism between X and Y, we say X and Y are isomorphic, denoted by X \cong Y. Isomorphism is an equivalence relation.
With isomorphism, we can define the cardinality of a set. Two isomorphic sets have the same cardinality.

Let X be a set and n \in \mathbb {N}. A si said to have cardinality n, denoted by |A|= n, if there exists an isomorphism between A and S_n = \{ 1,2,\cdots ,n \}. If A has finite cardinality, we say A is finite, otherwise we say A is infinite, denoted by |A| \geq \infty .
The next topic is the product of sets

Let X and Y be sets, then the Cartesian product of X and Y is the set
X \times Y = \set {(x,y) \mid x \in X \text { and } y \in Y}
There are two natural projections from the Cartesian product to the original sets, namely
\pi _1 : X \times Y \to X \text { and } \pi _2 : X \times Y \to Y
This leads to an important concept named universal property.
