fr:mainmatter.html:p: In this section we discuss the limits of variously-shaped diagrams of sets.
The pullback also satisfies the universal property.
We start constructing \mathbb {R} from \mathbb {Q} by a way that it satisfies the existence theorem, the core of construction.
There exists an ordered field \mathbb {R} that satisfies the least upper bound property. Moreover \mathbb {R} contains \mathbb {Q} as a subfield.
The least-upper-bound property mentioned above is defined:
A set S has the least upper bound property if every non-empty subset T of S that is bounded above has a least upper bound \sup T.

Why do we need the least-upper-bound property? Consider the set S = \{x \in \mathbb {Q} | x^2 < 2\}. S is bounded above by 2, but it does not have a least upper bound in \mathbb {Q}. Therefore we can't express \sqrt {2} in field \mathbb {Q} since some "gaps" exist. This fact motivates us to construct a more complete field \mathbb {R}. We have constructed \mathbb {Q} from \mathbb {Z}, and now we construct \mathbb {R} from \mathbb {Q}.

As we use set theory to construct \mathbb {R}, it motivates us to define Dedekind cut as a set. It should satisfies some properties:
Can't be empty or the whole \mathbb {Q}
Closed downward
Contains not the largest number A formal definition is given below:

A Dedekind cut is a partition of the rationals \mathbb {Q} into two non-empty sets L and R such that:
L\neq \emptyset
R\neq \emptyset
if x,y\in \mathbb {Q}, x<y and y\in L then x\in L
if p\in L then exists q\in L such that p<q
Now we can defined the real number as a set of Dedekind cuts.

The element of \mathbb {R} is a Dedekind Cut in \mathbb {Q}.
\mathbb {R} := \{ L | (L,R) \text { is a Dedekind Cut} \}

Now define the order relation on \mathbb {R}. We have defined \mathbb {R} as the set of Dedekind cuts, so we can define the strict partial order relation < on \mathbb {R} by the set operation \subset . The irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive properties are trivial.

General topology studies the structures that remain after distance, angle, and coordinates have been forgotten. What remains is a rule for deciding which subsets are open. From this rule one can recover a useful notion of nearness, formulate continuity without a metric, and compare spaces up to homeomorphism. The resulting language is broad enough to treat Euclidean spaces, function spaces, quotient constructions, and spaces that cannot be described by distances at all.

This note follows the order and conventions of the general-topology part of Munkres's Topology, with occasional comparison to the Stacks Project topology chapter. In particular, compactness means the finite-subcover property and does not include Hausdorffness.

A topology does not assign a numerical distance to two points. Instead, it records which collections of points may serve as observable regions. The three topology axioms say that these regions include the trivial ones and are stable under the unions and finite intersections needed to combine observations.

A topology on a set X is a collection \tau \subseteq \mathcal {P}(X) satisfying the following axioms:
\varnothing \in \tau and X\in \tau .
If \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq \tau , then \bigcup _{i\in I}U_i\in \tau .
If U_1,\ldots ,U_n\in \tau , then U_1\cap \cdots \cap U_n\in \tau . The pair (X,\tau ) is a topological space, and the members of \tau are its open sets. A subset F\subseteq X is closed when X\setminus F is open; it is clopen when it is both open and closed.

Let \tau _1 and \tau _2 be topologies on the same set X. The topology \tau _1 is finer, or stronger, than \tau _2 if
\tau _2\subseteq \tau _1.
Equivalently, \tau _2 is coarser, or weaker, than \tau _1. Thus a finer topology has more open sets and imposes a stronger continuity requirement on maps into the space.

Open sets describe the space globally. Near one fixed point it is more economical to work with neighborhoods, and for the entire topology it is often enough to specify a basis. These two reductions will later control continuity, countability, and product constructions.

Let X be a topological space and let x\in X. A subset N\subseteq X is a neighborhood of x if there is an open set U such that
x\in U\subseteq N.
In particular, a neighborhood need not itself be open.

A collection \mathcal {B}_x of neighborhoods of x is a local basis at x if every neighborhood N of x contains some B\in \mathcal {B}_x. A statement holds locally at x when it holds on some neighborhood of x.

Let (X,\tau ) be a topological space. A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \tau is a basis for \tau if, whenever U\in \tau and x\in U, there is some B\in \mathcal {B} such that
x\in B\subseteq U.
Equivalently, every open set is a union of members of \mathcal {B}.

A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \mathcal {P}(X) generates a topology by taking arbitrary unions of its members provided that it covers X and satisfies the refinement condition
x\in B_1\cap B_2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \exists B_3\in \mathcal {B},\; x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2.

A single set can carry many topologies. At the two extremes, the discrete topology declares every subset open, whereas the indiscrete topology retains only the opens forced by the axioms. Euclidean topology and, on an infinite set, cofinite topology provide less degenerate examples between these extremes.

Let X be a set. The discrete topology on X is the power set \mathcal {P}(X), so every subset is open. The indiscrete topology is \{\varnothing ,X\}, so only the two sets required by the topology axioms are open.
These are respectively the finest and coarsest topologies on the fixed underlying set X.

For n\geq 1, let
d(x,y)=\sqrt {\sum _{i=1}^{n}(x_i-y_i)^2}
be the Euclidean distance on \mathbb {R}^n. A subset U\subseteq \mathbb {R}^n is Euclidean open if, for every x\in U, there is some \varepsilon >0 such that
B_\varepsilon (x) =\{y\in \mathbb {R}^n\mid d(x,y)<\varepsilon \} \subseteq U.
The collection of Euclidean open subsets is the Euclidean topology on \mathbb {R}^n.
When n=1, the open balls are open intervals. Thus a subset U\subseteq \mathbb {R} is Euclidean open precisely when every x\in U lies in an interval (a,b)\subseteq U.
Let X be a set. The cofinite topology on X consists of \varnothing together with every subset U\subseteq X whose complement X\setminus U is finite.

Once spaces have been specified, the appropriate maps between them are those that respect open sets. The preimage formulation is deliberately asymmetric: it works for every function, preserves unions and intersections, and therefore composes without additional hypotheses.

Let (X,\tau _X) and (Y,\tau _Y) be topological spaces. A map f:X\to Y is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open:
V\in \tau _Y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f^{-1}(V)\in \tau _X.
Equivalently, the preimage of every closed subset of Y is closed in X. Continuity therefore depends on both the underlying function and the topologies placed on its domain and codomain.
Let \mathcal {B} be a basis for the topology of Y. A map f:X\to Y is continuous if and only if f^{-1}(B) is open in X for every B\in \mathcal {B}.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The forward implication follows immediately from continuity because every basis element is open. Conversely, suppose the preimage of each basis element is open. Every open subset V\subseteq Y is a union of basis elements, say V=\bigcup _{i\in I}B_i. Preimages preserve arbitrary unions, so
f^{-1}(V) =f^{-1}\left (\bigcup _{i\in I}B_i\right ) =\bigcup _{i\in I}f^{-1}(B_i).
The right-hand side is open in X; hence f is continuous.

fr:title.text: Identity and Composition of Continuous Maps

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Identity and Composition of Continuous Maps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The identity map on every topological space is continuous. If f:X\to Y and g:Y\to Z are continuous maps, then their composite g\circ f:X\to Z is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
For every open set U\subseteq X, one has \operatorname {id}_X^{-1}(U)=U, so the identity is continuous. If W\subseteq Z is open, then
(g\circ f)^{-1}(W)=f^{-1}\left (g^{-1}(W)\right ).
Continuity of g makes g^{-1}(W) open in Y, and continuity of f then makes its preimage open in X.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Continuity belongs to a map together with its domain and codomain topologies; it is not merely a property of the underlying formula. The identity between two differently topologized copies of the same set is the smallest example where this dependence becomes visible.

Put the Euclidean topology \tau _e and the cofinite topology \tau _c on the same underlying set \mathbb {R}. The identity function
\operatorname {id}:(\mathbb {R},\tau _e) \longrightarrow (\mathbb {R},\tau _c)
is continuous. Indeed, the complement of every cofinite open set is finite. Singletons are Euclidean closed, and finite unions of closed sets remain closed, so every cofinite open set is Euclidean open.

The identity in the reverse direction is not continuous. The interval (0,1) is Euclidean open, but its preimage under the identity is not cofinite open because \mathbb {R}\setminus (0,1) is infinite. Thus the same set-theoretic function can be continuous in one direction and discontinuous in the other.

A homeomorphism is the topological analogue of an isomorphism. It permits information to move continuously in both directions, so every property expressed solely in terms of the topology is preserved.

A homeomorphism between topological spaces X and Y is a bijective continuous map f:X\to Y whose inverse f^{-1}:Y\to X is also continuous. If such a map exists, X and Y are homeomorphic, written X\cong Y.

A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism: continuity controls preimages of open sets, whereas continuity of the inverse also requires the original map to preserve the topology in the opposite direction.

fr:title.text: The Real Line and an Open Interval Are Homeomorphic

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Real Line and an Open Interval Are Homeomorphic

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
The map
f:\mathbb {R}\longrightarrow (0,1), \qquad f(x)=\frac 12+\frac {1}{\pi }\arctan x
is a bijection. It is continuous, and its inverse
f^{-1}(t)=\tan \left (\pi \left (t-\frac 12\right )\right )
is continuous on (0,1). Hence f is a homeomorphism. Topologically, boundedness and total length do not distinguish the open interval from the whole real line.

Three constructions account for a large fraction of naturally occurring spaces. A subset inherits opens from an ambient space, a product is observed through its coordinate projections, and a quotient is obtained by identifying points. Their definitions are best read together using the comparison of topologies: subspace and product topologies are the coarsest topologies making the relevant maps continuous, while the quotient topology is the finest one detected by the quotient map.
Passing to a subspace changes the ambient meaning of openness. An endpoint can acquire an open one-sided neighborhood even though no such set is open in the real line itself.

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Subspace Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Subspace Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let A\subseteq X carry the subspace topology, and let \iota :A\hookrightarrow X be the inclusion. A map f:Z\to A is continuous if and only if \iota \circ f:Z\to X is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The inclusion is continuous: for every open U\subseteq X, its preimage is A\cap U, which is open in A. Thus the forward implication follows from closure under composition.
Conversely, suppose \iota \circ f is continuous. Every open subset of A has the form A\cap U for some open U\subseteq X, and
f^{-1}(A\cap U)=(\iota \circ f)^{-1}(U).
This set is open in Z, so f is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Give A=[0,1] the subspace topology inherited from the real line. Then the subset
\{x\in A\mid 0\leq x<1\}=A\cap (-1,1)
is open in A, although it is not open in \mathbb {R}. Likewise, \{x\in A\mid 0<x\leq 1\} is open in A. The word open therefore always refers to an ambient topological space.

The product topology permits observations in finitely many coordinates at a time. This finite-coordinate condition is invisible for ordinary finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces but is essential for infinite products.

Let \{X_i\}_{i\in I} be a family of topological spaces. The product topology on the Cartesian product \prod _{i\in I}X_i has as a basis the sets
\prod _{i\in I}U_i,
where each U_i is open in X_i and U_i=X_i for all but finitely many indices i. Equivalently, it is the coarsest topology that makes every coordinate projection
\pi _i:\prod _{j\in I}X_j\longrightarrow X_i
continuous.

For a finite product X_1\times \cdots \times X_n, the basic open sets are simply products U_1\times \cdots \times U_n of open sets. For an infinite product, the finite-coordinate restriction distinguishes the product topology from the generally finer box topology.

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Product Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Product Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X=\prod _{i\in I}X_i carry the product topology, with projections \pi _i:X\to X_i. A map f:Z\to X is continuous if and only if every coordinate map \pi _i\circ f:Z\to X_i is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
If f is continuous, each coordinate map is continuous because the projections are continuous. Conversely, suppose all coordinate maps are continuous. Every basic open subset of X can be written as
B=\bigcap _{k=1}^{n}\pi _{i_k}^{-1}(U_{i_k}),
where each U_{i_k} is open in X_{i_k}. Therefore
f^{-1}(B) =\bigcap _{k=1}^{n}(\pi _{i_k}\circ f)^{-1}(U_{i_k}),
a finite intersection of open subsets of Z. The basis criterion now shows that f is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For positive integers m,n, the coordinate-concatenation bijection
\mathbb {R}^m\times \mathbb {R}^n \longrightarrow \mathbb {R}^{m+n}, \qquad (x,y)\longmapsto (x_1,\ldots ,x_m,y_1,\ldots ,y_n)
is a homeomorphism from the product of the Euclidean topologies to the Euclidean topology on \mathbb {R}^{m+n}.

Around a point (x,y), Euclidean balls and products of Euclidean balls refine one another. More precisely,
B_{\frac {\varepsilon }{\sqrt {2}}}(x)\times B_{\frac {\varepsilon }{\sqrt {2}}}(y) \subseteq B_\varepsilon (x,y) \subseteq B_\varepsilon (x)\times B_\varepsilon (y).
The two sides therefore generate the same open neighborhoods.

A quotient reverses the direction of construction. Instead of restricting an existing topology, it asks which subsets of the target can be recognized as open after pulling them back to the source. Its universal property is the practical way to construct maps out of a quotient.

Let X be a topological space and let q:X\to Y be a surjection. The quotient topology on Y is defined by
U\subseteq Y\text { is open} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q^{-1}(U)\text { is open in }X.
With this topology, q is called a quotient map. It is the finest topology on Y for which q is continuous.

In particular, if \sim is an equivalence relation on X, the canonical surjection
q:X\longrightarrow X/{\sim }, \qquad x\longmapsto [x]
equips the quotient set X/{\sim } with a topology. The resulting topological space is the quotient space of X by \sim .

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Quotient Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Quotient Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let q:X\to Y be a quotient map. For every topological space Z, a map g:Y\to Z is continuous if and only if g\circ q:X\to Z is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
If g is continuous, then g\circ q is continuous by closure under composition. Conversely, suppose g\circ q is continuous and let W\subseteq Z be open. Then
q^{-1}\left (g^{-1}(W)\right ) =(g\circ q)^{-1}(W)
is open in X. The defining property of the quotient topology implies that g^{-1}(W) is open in Y. Hence g is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Connectedness asks whether a space can be decomposed into two open pieces without overlap. This is a global property: every sufficiently small portion of a space may look simple while the whole space still splits into disconnected pieces.
A separation of a topological space X is a pair of disjoint, nonempty open sets U,V\subseteq X such that X=U\cup V. The space X is connected if it admits no separation.
Equivalently, X is connected precisely when its only clopen subsets are \varnothing and X. In this note the empty space is regarded as connected, since it has no separation.
The least-upper-bound property of the real numbers prevents an interval from splitting at an omitted boundary point. This supplies the basic source of connected examples in analysis.

fr:title.text: Intervals in the Real Line Are Connected

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intervals in the Real Line Are Connected

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let I\subseteq \mathbb {R} be an interval: whenever a,b\in I and a<c<b, one also has c\in I. Then I, with the Euclidean subspace topology, is connected.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Suppose instead that I=U\cup V is a separation. Choose u\in U and v\in V; after exchanging the names if necessary, assume u<v. The interval property gives [u,v]\subseteq I. Set
S=U\cap [u,v], \qquad c=\sup S.
The supremum exists by the least-upper-bound property, and u\leq c\leq v, so c\in I.
The point c cannot lie in U. If c<v, openness of U in I would place points of U\cap [u,v] strictly above c, contradicting the definition of the supremum. If c=v, then membership in U would contradict v\in V and U\cap V=\varnothing . Hence c\in V.
Since V is open in I, some \varepsilon >0 satisfies
(c-\varepsilon ,c+\varepsilon )\cap I\subseteq V.
By the defining property of the supremum, there is some s\in S with c-\varepsilon <s\leq c. Since c\notin U, in fact s<c. But then s\in U\cap V, a contradiction. Thus no separation exists.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The next theorem makes connectedness useful under constructions. A continuous map may collapse points, but it cannot tear one connected space into a disconnected image.
If X is connected and f:X\to Y is continuous, then the image f(X), with its subspace topology, is connected.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
First regard f as a map \bar f:X\to f(X). This corestriction is continuous: if U=f(X)\cap O is open in the subspace f(X), with O open in Y, then
\bar f^{-1}(U)=f^{-1}(O),
which is open in X.
Suppose f(X)=U\cup V were a separation. Continuity of \bar f makes \bar f^{-1}(U) and \bar f^{-1}(V) open in X. They are disjoint and cover X; they are also nonempty because \bar f is surjective. They would therefore form a separation of X, contradicting connectedness.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Compactness replaces an arbitrary amount of local covering data by a finite amount. It is a topological finiteness condition, not a statement about numerical boundedness. Closed bounded intervals motivate the definition, but the definition continues to make sense in every topological space.

An open cover of a topological space X is a collection \mathcal {U} of open subsets such that
X=\bigcup _{U\in \mathcal {U}}U.
A finite subcover is a finite subcollection \mathcal {V}\subseteq \mathcal {U} such that
X=\bigcup _{V\in \mathcal {V}}V.
The finite subcollection may be empty.
The space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover. A subset K\subseteq X is compact when it is compact with its subspace topology.

Following Munkres, compactness here does not include the Hausdorff condition. Some texts call this property quasi-compactness and reserve compact for Hausdorff spaces with the finite-subcover property.

fr:title.text: Closed Intervals in the Real Line Are Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Closed Intervals in the Real Line Are Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For real numbers a\leq b, the closed interval [a,b]\subseteq \mathbb {R} is compact in the Euclidean topology.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The case a=b is immediate. Assume a<b, and let \mathcal {U} be an open cover of [a,b]. Define
S=\{x\in [a,b]\mid [a,x]\text { is covered by finitely many members of } \mathcal {U}\}.
A member of the cover containing a also contains a short interval to the right of a, so S is nonempty. It is bounded above by b; let c=\sup S, using the least-upper-bound property.
Suppose c<b. Choose U\in \mathcal {U} containing c. Since U is open in the subspace [a,b], some \varepsilon >0 satisfies
(c-\varepsilon ,c+\varepsilon )\cap [a,b]\subseteq U.
Choose x\in S with c-\frac {\varepsilon }{2}<x\leq c. A finite cover of [a,x], together with U, covers [a,y] for some y>c. This places y in S, contradicting that c is an upper bound. Hence c=b.
Finally choose a member of the cover containing b. For some \delta >0, it contains every x\in [a,b] satisfying b-\delta <x\leq b. Since b=\sup S, choose x\in S with b-\delta <x\leq b. A finite cover of [a,x] together with this last member covers all of [a,b]. Therefore every open cover has a finite subcover.

fr:title.text: Closed Subspaces of Compact Spaces Are Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Closed Subspaces of Compact Spaces Are Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every closed subspace A of a compact space X is compact.
If X is compact and f:X\to Y is continuous, then the image f(X), with its subspace topology, is compact.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Regard f as a map \bar f:X\to f(X). It is continuous because the preimage of a subspace-open set f(X)\cap O is f^{-1}(O), which is open in X.
Let \mathcal {U} be an open cover of f(X). The collection
\{\bar f^{-1}(U)\mid U\in \mathcal {U}\}
is an open cover of X. Choose a finite subcover \bar f^{-1}(U_1),\ldots ,\bar f^{-1}(U_n). Surjectivity of \bar f then implies that U_1,\ldots ,U_n covers f(X).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Hausdorffness and compactness do not imply one another. Hausdorffness requires distinct points to admit disjoint observations and thereby rules out several pathologies of coarse topologies. It passes to subspaces and products, though an arbitrary quotient of a Hausdorff space need not remain Hausdorff.

A topological space X is Hausdorff, or T_2, if any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. That is, for x,y\in X with x\neq y, there are open sets U,V\subseteq X such that
x\in U,\qquad y\in V,\qquad U\cap V=\varnothing .
Every subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff, and every product of Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff in the product topology.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let A\subseteq X, where X is Hausdorff, and choose distinct points x,y\in A. Disjoint open neighborhoods U,V\subseteq X of x and y restrict to disjoint open neighborhoods A\cap U and A\cap V in A. Thus A is Hausdorff.
Now let X=\prod _{i\in I}X_i, with every X_i Hausdorff, and choose distinct points x,y\in X. They differ in some coordinate i. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods U_i,V_i\subseteq X_i of x_i and y_i. Their inverse images \pi _i^{-1}(U_i) and \pi _i^{-1}(V_i) are disjoint open neighborhoods of x and y in X.

fr:title.text: Compact Subsets of Hausdorff Spaces Are Closed

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Compact Subsets of Hausdorff Spaces Are Closed

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If K is a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space X, then K is closed in X.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The empty subset is closed, so suppose K is nonempty. Fix x\in X\setminus K. For each y\in K, choose disjoint open sets U_y and V_y with y\in U_y and x\in V_y. The sets K\cap U_y form an open cover of the subspace K; compactness gives finitely many indices y_1,\ldots ,y_n for which U_{y_1},\ldots ,U_{y_n} cover K. Set
V=V_{y_1}\cap \cdots \cap V_{y_n}.
Then V is an open neighborhood of x disjoint from U_{y_1}\cup \cdots \cup U_{y_n}, and hence disjoint from K. Every point outside K therefore has an open neighborhood contained in X\setminus K. The complement is open, so K is closed.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Euclidean real line is Hausdorff but noncompact. In the other direction, an infinite cofinite space is compact and connected, yet it is not Hausdorff.

fr:title.text: A Hausdorff Space Need Not Be Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Hausdorff Space Need Not Be Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every Euclidean space \mathbb {R}^n, for n\geq 1, is Hausdorff. Given distinct points x,y, choose \varepsilon =d(x,y)/3. The Euclidean balls B_\varepsilon (x) and B_\varepsilon (y) are disjoint by the triangle inequality, so they separate the two points.

fr:title.text: An Infinite Cofinite Space Is Compact but Not Hausdorff

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An Infinite Cofinite Space Is Compact but Not Hausdorff

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X be infinite and carry the cofinite topology. Given an open cover of X, choose one nonempty member U_0. Its complement is finite. For each of the finitely many points outside U_0, choose one further member of the cover containing that point. Together with U_0, these sets form a finite subcover, so X is compact.

Any two nonempty open subsets of X intersect: the complement of their intersection is a union of two finite sets and cannot be all of the infinite set X. Distinct points therefore cannot have disjoint open neighborhoods. Hence X is not Hausdorff. The same observation shows that X is connected.

Compactness and Hausdorffness become especially effective when they occur on opposite sides of a continuous bijection. Compactness makes closed information survive the map, and Hausdorffness recognizes the image as closed. This supplies a widely used criterion for proving that a bijection is a homeomorphism.
Let f:X\to Y be a continuous bijection. If X is compact and Y is Hausdorff, then f is a homeomorphism.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let C\subseteq X be closed. It is compact by compactness of closed subspaces, and its image f(C) is compact by preservation of compactness. Since Y is Hausdorff, compact subsets are closed, so f(C) is closed in Y. Thus f is a closed map.
For the inverse map f^{-1}:Y\to X, the preimage of a closed set C\subseteq X is
(f^{-1})^{-1}(C)=f(C),
which is closed in Y. Hence f^{-1} is continuous, and f is a homeomorphism.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can now return to the quotient construction. Gluing the two endpoints of a compact interval produces a circle, and the criterion above turns the evident continuous bijection into a homeomorphism.

fr:title.text: The Circle as a Quotient of an Interval

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Circle as a Quotient of an Interval

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Let
S^1=\{z\in \mathbb {C}\mid |z|=1\}, \qquad q:[0,1]\longrightarrow S^1, \qquad q(t)=e^{2\pi i t}.
The map q identifies precisely the endpoints 0 and 1. Let p:[0,1]\to [0,1]/(0\sim 1) be the canonical quotient map. There is a unique bijection
\bar q:[0,1]/(0\sim 1)\longrightarrow S^1
such that \bar q\circ p=q.

Since q is continuous, the universal property of the quotient makes \bar q continuous. The interval [0,1] is compact by compactness of closed intervals, and its quotient is compact by preservation under continuous images. The circle is Hausdorff as a subspace of the Euclidean plane. Therefore the compact-to-Hausdorff criterion shows that \bar q is a homeomorphism:
[0,1]/(0\sim 1)\cong S^1.

A basis may still be too large for explicit arguments. The two standard countability axioms ask whether local neighborhoods or the entire topology can be controlled by countable data. The second condition is stronger because one global basis must work simultaneously at every point.
A topological space X is first-countable if every point x\in X has an at most countable local basis. It is second-countable if its topology has an at most countable basis.

These conditions constrain two different scales. First-countability gives a countable collection of tests near each individual point, while second-countability gives one countable collection of basic open sets for the whole space.
Every second-countable topological space is first-countable.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let \mathcal {B} be a countable basis for X. For each x\in X, set
\mathcal {B}_x=\{B\in \mathcal {B}\mid x\in B\}.
This is a countable collection of open neighborhoods of x. If N is any neighborhood of x, choose an open set U with x\in U\subseteq N. The basis property supplies B\in \mathcal {B}_x with x\in B\subseteq U\subseteq N. Therefore \mathcal {B}_x is a countable local basis at x.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Rational endpoints give a countable basis for the Euclidean real line. In contrast, an uncountable discrete space has a one-element local basis at every point but cannot have a countable global basis.

In the Euclidean real line, let
\mathcal {B} =\{(p,q)\mid p,q\in \mathbb {Q},\;p<q\}.
This collection is countable because \mathbb {Q}\times \mathbb {Q} is countable. It is a basis: whenever U is open and x\in U, there is an interval (a,b) with x\in (a,b)\subseteq U; density of the rationals gives p,q\in \mathbb {Q} with
a<p<x<q<b.
Thus x\in (p,q)\subseteq U. Hence \mathbb {R} is second-countable and, by second-countability implies first-countability, also first-countable.

fr:title.text: An Uncountable Discrete Space Is Not Second-Countable

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An Uncountable Discrete Space Is Not Second-Countable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X be an uncountable set with the discrete topology. For every x\in X, the one-element collection \{\{x\}\} is a local basis at x; hence X is first-countable.

On the other hand, every basis \mathcal {B} for X must contain every singleton. Indeed, since \{x\} is open, the basis property requires some B\in \mathcal {B} with
x\in B\subseteq \{x\},
and therefore B=\{x\}. Thus \mathcal {B} is uncountable, so X is not second-countable. This also shows why the two countability axioms are genuinely different.

First-countability explains why sequences suffice for many arguments in metric spaces. Without such a hypothesis, sequences alone may fail to detect closure or continuity; nets or filters are then the appropriate general substitutes.

A noncompact space may nevertheless look compact around each point. Local compactness records this intermediate situation. It is strong enough to support many constructions from analysis while still including open subsets of Euclidean spaces and manifolds.
A topological space X is locally compact at x\in X if there exists a compact subspace K\subseteq X that is a neighborhood of x. The space is locally compact if it is locally compact at every point.

This definition does not include the Hausdorff condition. In a different convention, some texts use locally compact to mean locally compact and Hausdorff. Outside the Hausdorff setting, several common formulations of local compactness need not be equivalent.

fr:title.text: The Real Line Is Locally Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Real Line Is Locally Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For each x\in \mathbb {R}, the closed interval K=[x-1,x+1] is compact by compactness of closed intervals. It contains the open interval (x-1,x+1), so K is a neighborhood of x. Therefore the Euclidean real line is locally compact.

Keeping Hausdorffness separate from local compactness makes the convention explicit. It also prevents equivalent formulations from the Hausdorff setting from being used automatically in spaces where those formulations may diverge.

The concepts above form the basic toolkit of point-set topology. Bases present topologies, continuous maps compare them, subspaces, products, and quotients construct new spaces, and connectedness, compactness, Hausdorffness, countability, and local compactness measure the resulting spaces. Natural next steps include stronger separation axioms, the Tychonoff theorem, metrization theorems, and compactifications.
This note introduces the concept of vector space. Refer to Linear Algebra Done Right.
The motivation for the definition of a vector space comes from the properties of vectors in Euclidean space \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {C}^n. The definition abstracts and generalizes these properties.

A vector space over a field F is a non-empty set V together with a binary operation and a binary function that satisfy the axioms listed below. In this context, the elements of V are commonly called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars.
Commutativity: \forall x, y \in V, x + y = y + x
Associativity: \forall x, y, z \in V, (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)
Additive Identity: \exists 0 \in V \text { such that } \forall x \in V, x + 0 = x
Multiplicative Identity: \forall x \in V, 1x = x
Additive Inverse: \forall x \in V, \exists y \in V \text { such that } x + y = 0
Distributivity: \forall x, y \in V, \forall c, d \in F, c(x + y) = cx + cy, (c + d)x = cx + dx
Elements of a vector space are called vectors or points.
When dealing with vector spaces, we usually interested only in subspaces. And the union of subspaces is rarely a subspace, thus we are more interested with sums of subspaces.

A subset U of a vector space V over a field F is called a subspace of V if U is itself a vector space over F with the operations of addition and scalar multiplication on V. The subset also satisfies the following axioms (vice versa):
Additive identity: 0\in U
Closure: \forall u,v\in U, u+v\in U
Closed Scalar multiplication: \forall u\in U, \forall c\in F, cu\in U
After that we can define the sum of subsets.
Let U_1, \dots , U_n be subsets of a vector space V. The sum of U_1, \dots , U_n is defined as U_1 + \dots + U_n = \{u_1 + \dots + u_n \mid u_i \in U_i\}.
The sum of subspaces is the smallest subspace that contains all the subspaces.

Every element in U_1 + \dots + U_n can be written as a sum of elements u_i in U_i:
u_1+\cdots +u_n
We will interested in cases where each vector in U_1 + \dots + U_n can be represented in the form above in only one way. This leads to the definition of direct sum.
This note introduces the concept of finite-dimensional vector space. Refer to Linear Algebra Done Right.
Adding up scalar multiples of vectors in a list gives a linear combination.

Let V be a vector space over a field F. Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in V. A linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n is an expression of the form
a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n
where a_1, \dots , a_n \in F.
To talk about a structure, we usually define a collection of this structure. Hence we have span for linear combinations.
If \text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_n) = V, we say that v_1, \dots , v_n spans V.

Suppose we have span S=\text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_n). (Span is trivially a subspace.) Obviously for all v_j (1 \leq j \leq n), v_j \in S. Because subspaces are closed under scalar multiplication and addition, every subspace of V containing v_1, \dots , v_n must contain S. Thus we conclude that S is the smallest subspace containing v_1, \dots , v_n.
The discussion about spans leads to a key definition in linear algebra.
A vector space V is called finite-dimensional if some list of vectors v_1, \dots , v_n spans V.
The opposite of finite-dimensional is infinite-dimensional.
A vector space V is called infinite-dimensional if it is not finite-dimensional.

Consider the situation that there is only one way to express a vector v as a linear combination of vectors in a list v_1, \dots , v_n. What property of the list v_1, \dots , v_n does this situation imply? The answer is linear independence.

A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly independent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 implies that a_1 = \dots = a_n = 0. The trivial case of \{0\} is also considered linearly independent.
If some vectors are not linearly independent, then there are more than one way to express a vector as a linear combination of vectors in the list. This leads to the following definition.
A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly dependent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 for some a_1, \dots , a_n \in \mathbb {F} with at least one a_i \neq 0 (not all 0).
The following lemma is a direct consequence of the definition of linear independence. It states that for a given linearly dependent list, we can always remove a vector without changing the span.

Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in a vector space V over a field \mathbb {F}. If v_1, \dots , v_n are linearly dependent, then there exists 1 \leq i \leq n such that
v_i \in \text {span}(v_1, \dots , v_{i-1})
Remove v_i from the list v_1, \dots , v_n and the span does not change

fr:title.text: Length of linearly independent list \leq length of spanning list

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Length of linearly independent list \leq length of spanning list

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a finite dimensional vector space, the length of a linearly independent list is less than or equal to the length of a spanning list.
We have discussed linear independent lists and spanning lists. Now we are ready to define a basis.
A basis of V is a list of vectors in V that is linearly independent and spans V.
Criterion for basis A list of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is a basis of V if and only if every v \in V can be written uniquely as a linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n.
For instance, we have standard basis \{e_1, \dots , e_n\} for \mathbb {F}^n, where e_i is the vector with 1 at i-th position and 0 elsewhere.
Every spanning list in a vector space can be reduced to a basis.
From the theorem we can infer a corollary.
Every finite-dimensional vector space has a basis.
The next result states for a spanning list can be reduced to a basis. We can adjoin one or more vectors to a linearly independent list to form a basis.

fr:title.text: Linearly dependent list extends to a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linearly dependent list extends to a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every linearly independent list of vectors in a finite-dimensional vector space can be extended to a basis.
Recall the definition of direct sum, we can now show that every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space can be paired with another subspace to form a direct sum of the whole space.

fr:title.text: Direct Sum of Subspaces of V

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Direct Sum of Subspaces of V

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Suppose V is a finite dimensional vector space, and U is a subspace of V. Then there exists a subspace W of V such that V = U \oplus W.

This post discusses about finite-dimensional vector space. But we have not yet defined what is dimension. We tempted to define the dimension as the length of basis intuitively. With this definition we should prove its well-definedness. That is, every basis has the same length.
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every basis of V has the same length.
This can be proved by Lemma 8. Now we can formally define the dimension of such spaces.
The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space V is the length of any basis of the vector space. Denoted by \dim V.
Every subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space is also finite-dimensional. Hence we can talk about the dimension of a subspace.
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and U be a subspace of V. Then \dim U \leq \dim V.

According to the definition of linearly independent, to show a list of vectors is a basis, we only need to show it is linearly independent, and it spans the whole space. The next theorems simplifies the task:

fr:title.text: Linearly independent list of the right length is a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linearly independent list of the right length is a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every linearly independent list of vectors in V with length equal to \dim V is a basis of V.

fr:title.text: Spanning list of the right length is a basis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spanning list of the right length is a basis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then every spanning list of vectors in V with length equal to \dim V is a basis of V.
Now we move to the discussion of the dimension of the sum of two subspaces. This is analogous to the inclusion-exclusion principle.

Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and U and W be subspaces of V. Then
\dim (U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim (U \cap W).
This note introduces the concept of linear maps. Refer to Linear Algebra Done Right.

Now we arrive at the main topic of this chapter: linear maps. In classic mathematics, to understand the properties of the structure or space, we often study the maps between them. For vector spaces we study the linear maps.

A linear map is a function between two vector spaces that preserves the operations of addition and scalar multiplication. In other words, a function T: V \to W where V,W are vector spaces if the following conditions are satisfied:
Additivity: T(u+v) = T(u) + T(v) for all u,v \in V
Homogeneity: T(\alpha v) = \alpha T(v) for all \alpha \in \mathbb {F} and v \in V Sometimes we ignore the brackets and write T v instead of T(v).

Now we can talk about the set of all linear maps between two vector spaces.
\mathcal {L}(V,W) = \{ T: V \to W | T \text { is a linear map} \}

Define D\in \mathcal {L}(\mathcal {P}(\mathbb {R}),\mathcal {P}(\mathbb {R})) (recall that \mathcal {P} means set of polynomials) by
D(f) = f'
We can see that D a linear map.
Additivity: D(f+g) = (f+g)' = f' + g' = D(f) + D(g)
Homogeneity: D(\alpha f) = (\alpha f)' = \alpha f' = \alpha D(f)

Let V be the vector space of all continuous functions on the interval [a,b]. The map I: V \to V defined by
I(f) = \int _a^x f(t) dt
is a linear map. In other words, I preserves the operations of addition and scalar multiplication: For all f,g \in V and all \alpha \in \mathbb {R},
I(f+g) = I(f) + I(g) \quad \text {and} \quad I(\alpha f) = \alpha I(f)
We can find a linear map that takes on whatever values we wish on the vectors in a basis by the following theorem.

fr:title.text: Linear maps and basis of domain

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linear maps and basis of domain

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Let v_1, v_2, \ldots , v_n be a basis of vector space V. Then for any vector space W and any vectors w_1, w_2, \ldots , w_n in W, there exists a unique linear map T: V \to W such that
T(v_i) = w_i \quad \text {for all} \quad i = 1,2,\ldots ,n

Now let's turn to the algebraic operations over the set of linear maps \mathcal {L}(V,W). We begin by defining the addition and scalar multiplication of linear maps. This leads to a surprising result: the set of linear maps is actually a vector space.

Let T_1, T_2 \in \mathcal {L}(V,W). We define the addition of T_1 and T_2 as the linear map T_1 + T_2: V \to W such that
(T_1 + T_2)(v) = T_1(v) + T_2(v) \quad \text {for all} \quad v \in V
The scalar multiplication of a linear map T \in \mathcal {L}(V,W) by a scalar c \in \mathbb {F} is the linear map cT: V \to W such that
(cT)(v) = cT(v) \quad \text {for all} \quad v \in V
With these operations, \mathcal {L}(V,W) is a vector space over the field \mathbb {F}. Note that the additive identity of \mathcal {L}(V,W) is the zero map 0: V \to W such that
0(v) = 0 \quad \text {for all} \quad v \in V

Usually it makes no sense to multiply two linear maps. But we can define an operation called the product of linear maps, which is just the composition of the two functions. This can form a monoid or even a group under certain conditions.

Let T_1: V \to W and T_2: W \to U be linear maps. We define the product of T_1 and T_2 as the linear map T_2 \circ T_1: V \to U such that
(T_2 \circ T_1)(v) = T_2(T_1(v)) \quad \text {for all} \quad v \in V
Note that this is just the composition of the two functions T_1 and T_2. And we usually denote T_2 \circ T_1 by T_2T_1. The product of linear maps is associative, that is,
(T_3 \circ T_2) \circ T_1 = T_3 \circ (T_2 \circ T_1)
for any linear maps T_1: V \to W, T_2: W \to U, and T_3: U \to X. The identity map I_V: V \to V is the identity element of the set of linear maps \mathcal {L}(V,V) under the product operation. That is, for any linear map T: V \to V,
I_V \circ T = T \circ I_V = T
where I_V is the identity map on V. The set of all linear maps from a vector space to itself, \mathcal {L}(V,V), forms a monoid under the product operation. The set of all invertible linear maps from a vector space to itself, \mathcal {L}(V,V)^*, forms a group under the product operation. The identity map is the identity element of the group \mathcal {L}(V,V)^*.

With addition we also have the distributive law for the product of linear maps. That is, for any linear maps S,S_1,S_2: V \to W and T,T_1,T_2: U\to V:
(S_1 + S_2)T = S_1T + S_2T \quad \text {and} \quad T(S_1 + S_2) = TS_1 + TS_2
In algebra, we have a structure named kernel, which is the set of all elements that are mapped to the zero element. For linear maps, the kernel is the null space
The injective linear map is defined like normal injective functions. To check whether a linear map is injective, we can just check whether the null space is trivial.
Let T: V \to W be a linear map. Then T is injective if and only if \text {null } T = \{ 0 \}.
The image of a linear map is the set of all elements that are mapped to by some element in the domain. This is called the range of the linear map, just like range of normal function.
If T: V \to W is a linear map, then the range of T is a subspace of W.
The next theorem plays a crucial role in the study of linear maps.

Let V be finite-dimensional vector space and T : V \to W be a linear map. Then \text {range } T is finite-dimensional and
\dim V = \dim \text {range } T + \dim \text {null } T

Now we can show that no linear map from a finite-dimensional vector space to a smaller (In dimension) vector space can be injective. This can be easily proved by the fundamental theorem of linear maps.

fr:title.text: Map to smaller dimension is not injective

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Map to smaller dimension is not injective

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces, and \dim V > \dim W. Then no linear map T:V\to W is injective.
Similarly, we can show that no linear map from a finite-dimensional vector space to a larger (In dimension) vector space can be surjective.

fr:title.text: Map to bigger dimension is not surjective

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Map to bigger dimension is not surjective

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces, and \dim V < \dim W. Then no linear map T:V\to W is surjective.
These two lemmas are very important in the study of linear equations. The idea here is to express linear equations system in terms of linear maps.
Rephrase in terms of a linear map the question of whether a homogeneous system linear equations has a nonzero solution.
A homogeneous system of linear equations with more variables than equations has a nontrivial solution.
We have seen that map to smaller dimension is not injective. T is not injective if n > m. This results the theorem above.
Rephrase in terms of a linear map the question of whether a inhomogeneous system linear equations has no solutions for some choice of constant terms.
An inhomogeneous system of linear equations with more equations than variables has no solution for some choice of the constant term.

Let v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n be a basis of V. We know that for any value of a linear map T:V\to W, can be determined by values \{ T(v_1), T(v_2), \cdots , T(v_n) \}. This leads to the definition of the matrix representation of a linear map.
Now we can define the matrix representation of a linear map.

Let T\in \mathcal {L}(V,W), \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_n \}\subset V be a basis of V, and \{ w_1,\ldots ,w_m \}\subset W be a basis of W. The matrix of T with respect to these bases is the m\times n matrix \mathcal {M}(T) such that
T(v_j) = \sum _{i=1}^m \mathcal {M}(T)_{ij}w_i
Or we denote \mathcal {M}(T) as \mathcal {M}(T, (v_1,\ldots ,v_n), (w_1,\ldots ,w_m)).
If T maps n-dimensional vector space to m-dimensional vector space, then \mathcal {M}(T) is a m\times n matrix.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
For two same-size matrix A,B, the sum of A and B is the matrix C such that
C_{ij} = A_{ij} + B_{ij}
In the language of linear maps S,T\in \mathcal {L}(V,W),
\mathcal {M}(T+S) = \mathcal {M}(T) + \mathcal {M}(S)

For a scalar c and a matrix A, the product of c and A is the matrix B such that
B_{ij} = cA_{ij}
In the language of linear maps T\in \mathcal {L}(V,W),
\mathcal {M}(cT) = c\mathcal {M}(T)
The set of all m\times n matrices with elements in \mathbb {F} is denoted as \mathcal {M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb {F}) or \mathbb {F}^{m\times n}.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can see that \mathbb {F}^{m\times n} is itself a vector space.
\mathbb {F}^{m\times n} is a vector space with dimension mn.

Consider linear maps T:U\to V and S:V\to W. The composition of linear maps is ST. Does the composition of linear maps have a matrix representation?
\mathcal {M}(ST) = \mathcal {M}(S)\mathcal {M}(T)
This makes no sense now but indicates the definition of matrix multiplication.
Now we see that the desired matrix multiplication holds. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general. However, it satisfies the associative law and the distributive law.

Let A be a m\times n matrix.
If 1\leq j\leq m then A_{j\cdot } is the j-th row of A, defined as a 1\times n matrix. (A row vector)
If 1\leq j\leq n then A_{\cdot j} is the j-th column of A, defined as a m\times 1 matrix. (A column vector)
With the notation we can think of matrix multiplication in another perspective.
We have an interesting observation.
Now we begin the study the invertibility of linear maps.
An isomorphism is a linear map that is invertible. Two vector spaces are said to be isomorphic if there exists an isomorphism between them.
A linear map is invertible if and only if it is bijective.
Two finite-dimensional vector spaces over \mathbb {F} are isomorphic iff they have the same dimension.
Let v_1, v_2, \ldots , v_n be a basis for V, and w_1, w_2, \ldots , w_m be a basis for W. Then \mathcal {M} is an isomorphism between \mathcal {L}(V,W) and \mathbb {F}^{m\times n}.
This has a trivial corollary.

Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces. Then \mathcal {L}(V,W) is finite-dimensional and
\dim (\mathcal {L}(V,W)) = \dim (V)\dim (W).
This note is about the category theory and its applications. Instead of reading a well-organized book, I prefer to write down the things I learned from ncatlab and papers.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Intuitively, a category is a collection of objects and arrows between them, such arrows can be composed and there is an identity arrow for each object.
There are commonly two ways to define a category, which are equivalent in usual foundations of mathematics. One of them generalizes the notion of internal category nicely while the other one is more convenient for enriched category.
The major difference is whether they use a single collection of all morphisms or several collections of morphisms (family of collections indexed by pairs of objects)

A category C consists
A collection of objects C_0 (\text {Ob}(C)).
A collection C_1 (\text {Mor}(C)) of morphisms (arrows).
For every morphism f there are an object s(f) (source, domain) and an object t(f) (target, codomain).
For every pair of morphisms f, g such that t(f) = s(g), there is a morphism g \circ f (composition) (Also written gf or f;g).
For every object x, there is a morphism \text {id}_x (or 1_x) called identity.
The following properties hold:
s(g \circ f) = s(f) and t(g \circ f) = t(g).
s(1_x) = x and t(1_x) = x.
Composition is associative: h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f when t(f) = s(g), and t(g) = s(h).
Composition satisfies the identity laws: f \circ \text {id}_x = f and \text {id}_y \circ f = f If the identity map and its axioms are omitted then one speaks of a semicategory.

fr:title.text: With a family of collections of morphisms
fr:title.html:strong: With a family of collections of morphisms

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
A category C consists
A collection of objects C_0 (\text {Ob}(C)).
For every pair of objects x, y, a collection C_1(x, y) (\hom _C(x,y)) of morphisms from x to y.
For each pair of morphisms f in C_1(x,y) and g in C_1(y,z), a morphism g \circ f in C_1(x,z). called their composition.
For each object x, a morphism \text {id}_x in C_1(x,x) called the identity on x.
The following properties hold:
Composition is associative: h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f for all f in C_1(x,y), g in C_1(y,z), and h in C_1(z,w).
Composition satisfies the identity laws: f \circ \text {id}_x = f and \text {id}_y \circ f = f for all f in C_1(x,y). Usually we write \text {Mor}(C) for the disjoint union \bigsqcup _{x,y \in C_0} C_1(x,y).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Its common to talk about some objects and their morphisms. Informally, a diagram in a category C consists of some objects of C connected by some morphisms of C.
This terminology is often used when speaking about limits or colimits of a diagram.
One formal way to define a diagram is to use a functor from a (very) small category to C. That is, a functor whose domain is a small category.
A category is said to be small if it has a small set (i.e. a set but not a proper class) of objects and morphisms. In other words a small category is an internal category in category of sets.

We did not explain what a functor is, but it is very natural thought. Briefly, a functor is a homomorphism between two categories. It maps objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms, preserving the structure of the categories.

A functor F from a category C to a category D is a map sending each x\in C to an object F(x)\in D and each morphism f:x\to y in C to morphism F(f):F(x)\to F(y) in D, such that
Composition is preserved: F(g\circ f) = F(g)\circ F(f).
Identity is preserved: F(\text {id}_x) = \text {id}_{F(x)}.
For the sake of completeness, we state the definition of the functor category and the natural transformations between functors.

Let C and D be categories, the functor category D^C (or [C,D]) is the category whose
objects are functors from C to D.
morphisms are natural transformations between functors.
We state the concise functorial definition of diagrams of the shape of categories.
Let C be a category and J be a small category. A diagram of shape J in C is a functor X:J\to C. The category of J-shaped diagrams in C is the functor category C^J.
A limit of a diagram F:D\to C is an object \lim F of C equipped with morphisms to the objects F(d) for all d\in D, such that everything in sight commutes.

html:ul.html:li: An object (c,c') \in C^{\text {op}} \times C is mapped to the set \hom _C(c, c') in \text {Set}, the set of morphisms c \to c' in C.

A morphism (f,g) : (c, c') \to (d, d') in the product category will be sent to the function \hom _C((f,g)) : \hom _C(c, c') \to \hom _C(d, d') which maps
h \mapsto g \circ h \circ f

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Representability is one of the most fundamental concepts of category theory, with close ties to the notion of adjoint functor and the Yoneda lemma. It is the crucial concept underlying the idea of universal property.

For a locally small category C, a presheaf on C, which is of the form F : C^{\text {op}} \to \text {Set}, is representable if it is natural isomorphic to a hom-functor h_X: \hom _C(-, X) for some object X in C, which sends an object U\in C to the hom-set \hom _C(U,X). The object is determined uniquely up to isomorphism in C, and is called a representing object of the presheaf F.

Let C and D be categories, let L : C \to D and R : D \to C be functors, then this is called a pair of adjoint functors with L left adjoint and R right adjoint, denoted L \dashv R, if there exists a natural isomorphism between the hom-functors of the following form:
\hom _D(L(-), -) \cong \hom _C(-, R(-))
which means \forall c\in C, d\in D there is a bijection of hom-sets:
\begin {align*} \hom _D(L(c), d) &\xrightarrow {\cong } \hom _C(c, R(d)) \\ \{ L(c) \xrightarrow {f} d \} &\mapsto \{ c \xrightarrow {\hat {f}} R(d) \} \end {align*}
which is natural in both c and d. This isomorphism is the adjunction isomorphism and the image \bar {f} of a morphism f under this isomorphism is called the adjunct of f, and vice versa.

Consider a pair of adjoint functors L \dashv R, \forall c\in C the adjunct of the identity morphism \text {id}_{L(c)} is the unit morphism of the adjunction at that object, denoted by
\eta _c = \hat {\text {id}_{L(c)}} : c \to R(L(c))
and the adjunct of the identity morphism \text {id}_{R(d)} is the counit morphism of the adjunction at that object, denoted by
\varepsilon _d = \text {id}_{R(d)} : L(R(d)) \to d

Now we reach an important theorem in category theory, the Yoneda lemma, an elementary but central result in category theory, sheaf and topos theory. It says that the set of morphism from a representable presheaf into an arbitrary presheaf X is in natural bijection with set X(c) assigned by X to the representing object c.

For a locally small category C, we denote [C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}] := \text {Func}(C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}) for the functor category out of the opposite category of C into \text {Set}, the category of sets. This is also called the presheaf category of C. The functor Y : C \to [C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}] defined by
c \mapsto \hom _C(-, c)
from C to its presheaf category is called the Yoneda embedding, which sends each object of c into the hom-functor into that object, also called the presheaf represented by c.

From the exponential we know that the Yoneda embedding is just the adjunct of the hom-functor \hom _C(-, -) under the functor category adjunction:
\hom (C ^{\text {op}} \times C, \text {Set}) \cong \hom (C, [C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}])
in the closed symmetric monoidal category

Let C be a locally small category, with the presheaf category [C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}]. For any presheaf X \in [C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}], there is a canonical isomorphism
\hom _{[C^{\text {op}}, \text {Set}]}(\hom _C(-, c), X) \cong X(c)
between the hom-set of presheaf morphism from the representable presheaf h_c = \hom _C(-,c) to X, and the value of X at c.
This is a note about the the argument that JavaScript is an untyped language. Most opinions came from the References.

The first thing I want to classify is the word strong typing and weak typing are meaningless. In a limit case we can compare two languages that have similar type system, and talk about which one is stronger. But for the common case, it's totally nonsense.

Static and dynamic typing is a meaningful classsification. But the discussion about dynamic and static languages is mostly wrong on the Internet. Dynamic language is a popular concept, however, it is rather a marketing than a well-defined terminology. It's designed to confuse rather than inform.

In fact, dynamic typing is just a special case of static typing. It limits more than contributes.The root of the problem is the confusion between type and class. It's very useful to have multiple classes of values of a same type. They are interchangeable because they represent values of the same type. Only the form of presentation differs.

The distinction between two classes of the same type is dynamic. But this does not conflict with the fact that only one static type. In type theory this is what we called Sum Type. Being a sum type we can dispatch on the class of the value of the type, and decide what to do at runtime.

This characteristics is same to dynamic language where values can be classified into various forms that can be distinguished at runtime. The answer is now clear: dynamic language classifies all values in this way. What they do just merge all values of the language into a single type. The so-called untyped language is just unityped.
Therefore, JavaScript is definitely untyped.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Giving two functions f, g we can compose then to get a new function f\circ g = f(g(x)). Using \lambda -notation, we can define the composition of two functions as follows:
f\circ g = \lambda x.f(g(x))
And the composition operation is also a lambda abstraction.
\circ = B = \lambda f.\lambda g.\lambda x.f(g(x))
Composing identity function with any function does not change the function. We expect the following equation to hold:
f\circ I = f = I\circ f
where I is the identity function. This can be verified by the following calculation:
\begin {align*} B\space f\space I &= (\lambda f.\lambda g.\lambda x.f(g(x)))\space f\space I \\ &\to _\beta \lambda g.\lambda x.f(g(x))\space I \\ &\to _\beta \lambda x.f(I(x)) \\ &\to _\beta \lambda x.f(x) \\ &=_\eta f \end {align*}
The last step requires an extensional equality, which is the called eta-conversion.
\text {for}\space x\not \in \text {FV}(f) ,\lambda x.f(x) =_\eta f
It makes more sense to use the equation from right to left called eta-expansion (And more discipline has to be imposed or expansion does not terminate).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The well-known divergent combinator implies that the lambda calculus is not strongly normalizing.

However, we can always compute a normal form if one exists. Though there are many reduction strategies, there is a complete one for expressions that have normal form. This kind of reduction strategy is called normal order reduction or leftmost-outermost reduction. It scans through the expression from left to right and when it find a redex, it reduces it by applying beta reduction and returns to the beginning.
The notation of leftmost-outermost reduction is closely related to the notion of call-by-name evaluation in programming languages. (A little more distance to call-by-need evaluation in Haskell)
In contrast, call-by-value evaluation is not complete, which would reduce the argument of a function before applying beta reduction.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The outcome of a computation e is its normal form. It is naturally to ask the question whether the normal form is unique. The key to this question is the Church-Rosser property or confluence: If e\to ^* e_1 and e\to ^* e_2, then there exists a term e_3 such that
e_1\to ^* e_3\space \text {and}\space e_2\to ^* e_3
This implies the uniqueness of the normal form.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can represent natural numbers in lambda calculus by using the Church numerals or Church encoding. The two abstractions should be related in some ways: one x stands for zero and the other f stands for the successor function.

The Church numeral n is a function that takes two arguments f and x and applies f to x n times. The Church numeral 0 is defined as the identity function \lambda f.\lambda x.x. The Church numeral 1 is defined as the successor of 0:
1 = \lambda f.\lambda x.f(x)
The Church numeral 2 is defined as the successor of 1:
2 = \lambda f.\lambda x.f(f(x))
And so on.

The Church numeral n is defined as the successor of n-1:
n = \lambda f.\lambda x.f^n(x)
where f^n(x) means applying f to x n times.

The successor function is defined as follows:
S = \lambda n.\lambda f.\lambda x.f(n\space f\space x)

Using the iteration property we can define mathematical functions over the natural numbers in lambda calculus. The addition of two Church numerals m and n is defined as follows:
m+n = \lambda n.\lambda k. n\space S\space k

The multiplication of two Church numerals m and n is defined by iterating the addition function m times:
m*n = \lambda n.\lambda k. n\space (k + ) \space 0

The exponentiation of two Church numerals m and n is defined as follows:
m^n = \lambda m.\lambda n. n\space (m *) \space 1

As we saw before, a natural number n is represented by a function that iterates its first argument n times on its second argument.
n = \lambda g.\lambda c.g^n(c)
Another way to specify such a function schematically is
\begin {align*} f \space 0 &= c \\ f (n+1) &= g\space (f\space n) \end {align*}
If such a function satisfies such a schema of iteration, then it can be defined in the lambda calculus on Church numerals as
f = \lambda n.n \space g \space c
This definition is total which means it is defined for all natural numbers. Let's define the multiplication again
\begin {align*} m*0 &= 0 \\ m*(n+1) &= m + (m*n) \end {align*}
To fit our schema of iteration, we can define the multiplication by abstracting over k:
\begin {align*} \text {times}\space 0 &= \lambda k.0 \\ \text {times}\space (n+1) &= \lambda k.k + (\text {times}\space n\space k) \end {align*}
where the c and g are
\begin {align*} c &= \lambda k.0 \\ g &= \lambda r.\lambda k.k+(r\space k) \end {align*}
and we obtain
\text {times} = \lambda n.n(\lambda rk. k + (r\space k))(\lambda k.0)

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
General Recursion
Let's first consider the greatest common divisor function \gcd (a,b)
\begin {align*} \gcd \space a\space a &= a \\ \gcd \space a\space b &= \gcd \space (a-b)\space b \text { if } b > a \\ \gcd \space a\space b &= \gcd \space a\space (b-a) \text { if } a > b \end {align*}
This recursion is terminating because the arguments are decreasing. We can deal with this case currently and let's be hold. We consider the most general schema of recursion.
f = h\space f
which means that in the right-hand side we can make arbitrary recursive calls to the function f. For \gcd we have
h = \lambda gab. \text {if } (a=b)\space a\space (( \text {if }\space (a>b)\space (g\space (a-b)\space b)\space (g\space a\space (b-a)) ))
How can we define f explicitly when given h so that f = h\space f, which called a fixed point pf h. If we believe Church-Turing thesis, then any partial recursive function should be representable on Church numerals in lambda calculus. Hence we can find such f and the answer is called Y-combinator. We want that if f = Y\space h and f=h\space f, so we get Y\space h = h \space (Y\space h).
Y\space h = h\space (Y\space h) = h\space (h\space (Y\space h)) = h\space (h\space (h\space (Y\space h))) = \cdots
This iterates infinitely. The definition of Y is:
Y = \lambda h.(\lambda x. h\space (x\space x))\space (\lambda x. h\space (x\space x))
The application x\space x will replicate Y\space h:
\begin {align*} Y\space h &= (\lambda x. h\space (x\space x))\space (\lambda x. h\space (x\space x)) \\ &= h\space ((\lambda x. h\space (x\space x))\space (\lambda x. h\space (x\space x))) \\ &= h\space (Y\space h) \end {align*}
The partial recursive functions include functions that are undefined (have no normal form) on some arguments, hence we can't always find an answer. Consider f=f as a recursion schema and h=\text {id}.
Y\space h = Y\space \text {id} = (\lambda x. \text {id}\space (x\space x))\space (\lambda x. \text {id}\space (x\space x)) = (\lambda x. x\space x)\space (\lambda x. x\space x) = \Omega
The function f=\Omega solves the equation f=f by giving a divergent result.

Define Functions By Recursion
Consider the factorial function:
\text {fact}\space n = \text {if } (n=0)\space 1\space (n\space \text {fact}\space (n-1))
This requires a test \text {if0} satisfies:
\begin {align*} \text {if0}(0,c,d) &=c\\ \text {if0}(n+1,c,d) &=d \end {align*}
We can define \text {if0} by (Recall that K=\lambda xy.x):
\text {if0} = \lambda ncd. n\space (K\space d)\space c
The argument of Y combinator is defined:
h_\text {fact} = \lambda g. \lambda n. \text {if0}\space n\space 1\space (n\space g\space (n-1))
and
\text {fact} = Y\space h_\text {fact}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The scanner's task is to transform a stream of characters into a stream of words in the input language. Each word must be classified into a syntactic category. This note refers to Engineering a compiler
The first stage of a compiler is to perform lexical analysis by a scanner. The parser or syntax analyzer will fit the stream of words to a grammatical model of the input language.

Scanner construction has a strong foundation in formal language theory. Scanners are based on recognizers that simulate deterministic finite automata. We can specify the lexical structure using a set of regular expression.

Each time a scanner recognizes a word, it will return a token that contains the word (lexeme) and its syntactic category. The scanner uses microsyntax (the lexical structure of a language) to find and classify words. Keywords are identifiers but have special meanings.
A char-by-char algorithm to recognize words is trivial. Consider we want to recognize the word new. We can write down the following code.
We can also represent the code fragment using the simple transition diagram.
Transition diagrams can be viewed as formal mathematics objects called finite automata.

A finite automata (FA) is a five-tuple (S,\Sigma ,\delta ,s_0,S_A) where
S is the finite set of states in the recognizer including s_e, the error state.
\Sigma is the finite alphabet used by the recognizer. \Sigma is the union of the edge labels in the transition diagram.
\delta (s, c) is the recognizer's transition function, which maps each state s\in S and character c\in \Sigma into some next state. In state s_i with input character c the FA takes the transition s_i \xrightarrow {c} \delta (s_i, c).
s_0\in S is the initial state of the recognizer.
S_A is the set of accepting states, S_A\subseteq S.
\delta is only partially defined. For all other combinations of the state s_i and input char c we can define \delta (s_i,c)=s_e.
An FA accepts a string x and iff starting in s_0, the sequence of chars in x takes the FA to an accepting state when the entire string has been consumed.

The char-by-char model is very simple and now we consider about numbers. For simplicity, we consider only unsigned integers: An unsigned integer is either zero or series of one or more digits where the first one is non-zero.

The set of words accepted by a finite automata F forms a language L(F). The transition diagram of F specifies the syntactic structure of L(F). But such representation is complex and non-intuitive. Most systems use a notation called regular expressions to specify the language. Any language described by an RE is considered a regular language. RE is equivalent to FA.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Simply Typed Lambda Calculus and Representation Theorems

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We have explored the power of lambda calculus. Church's original purpose of the pure calculus of functions was a new foundations of mathematics distinct from set theory. Unfortunately the original lambda calculus is inconsistent (Every proposition has a proof). Church returned to the ideas by Russell and Whitehead and developed the Church's Simple Theory of Types. SLTC is a typed interpretation of the lambda calculus with only one type constructor \to that builds function types.

We follow the converntion that function type constructor \to is right-associative. We write e:\tau if expression e has type \tau .
\lambda x.x:\tau \to \tau
But the type is not unique. The booleans can be typed:
\begin {align*} \text {true} &= \lambda x.\lambda y.x : \alpha \to (\beta \to \alpha )\\ \text {false} &= \lambda x.\lambda y.y : \alpha \to (\beta \to \beta ) \end {align*}

We can record the types of variable in a typing context.
\Gamma :\equiv x_1:\tau _1,\ldots ,x_n:\tau _n
And we always assume that all variables declared in a context are distinct. This avoids any ambiguity when we try to determine the type of a variable. The typing judgment now becomes
\Gamma \vdash e:\tau
Are there expressions that cannot be typed in the simple type system? Yes, for example, \Omega =\lambda x.x\space x cannot be typed. But how do we prove that \Omega cannot be typed?

We can apply the typing rules and get a contradiction. \Omega is a lambda abstraction hence we can assume that it has type \tau \to \sigma . Then x has type \tau and x\space x has type \sigma . By the application of x\space x we get that \tau =\tau \to \sigma , which does not exist.

To recover from this in full generality we need recursive types.
\tau =F\tau
where F=\lambda \alpha .\alpha \to \sigma and we might have a solution with \tau =Y\space F. But such solution is not available to us. We do not have function from types to types F and a type level Y combinator. However it is ok to construct recursive types (we would do later).
We now show that the representation of the booleans is correct.
If \emptyset \vdash e:\alpha \to (\alpha \to \alpha ) and e is a normal form, then e = \text {true} or e = \text {false}.
We will later combine this with the following theorems which yields correctness of the representation of the booleans.
If \Gamma \vdash e:\tau then e\to _{\beta }^*e' for a normal form e'. And we can define subject reduction, if \Gamma \vdash e:\tau and e\to _{\beta }e' then \Gamma \vdash e':\tau .

Our characterization of normal forms is quite simple: terms that do not reduce. However, this is a negative condition, which is difficult to work with in proofs. We would like to have a positive condition, which is easier to work with.

We tend to give definitions in the form of inference rules. The property then holds if the judgment can be derived using the rules. (This closely related to the inductive deefintion). Before defining the normal forms we formally define beta reduction. The judgment here e\to e' expressing that e reduces to e'.
\begin {align*} \frac {}{(\lambda x.e_1)e_2\to e_1[x:=e_2]} (\text {red/beta}) \\ \frac {e\to e'}{\lambda x.e \to \lambda x.e'} (\text {red/lam}) \\ \frac {e_1\to e_1'}{e_1\space e_2\to e_1'\space e_2} (\text {red/app}_1) \\ \frac {e_2\to e_2'}{e_1\space e_2\to e_1\space e_2'} (\text {red/app}_2) \end {align*}

A normal form is an expression that does not reduce. To give a proper formalization,, we need a separate judgment for neutral terms which do not create a redex when applied to an argument.
\begin {align*} \frac {e\text { normal}}{\lambda x.e\text { normal}} (\text {normal/lam}) \\ \frac {e\text { neutral}}{e\text { normal}} (\text {normal/var}) \\ \frac {}{x\text { neutral}} (\text {neutral/var}) \\ \frac {e_1\text { neutral}\quad e_2\text { normal}}{e_1\space e_2\text { neutral}} (\text {neutral/app}) \\ \end {align*}

The characterization of normal forms via inference rules is compact, but is it really the same as saying that an expression does not reduce? We break this down into the following two properties.
For all expressions e, either e reduces or e is normal
For all expressions e, it is not that case e reduces and e is normal
We have theorem that ensures that the first property holds. (Proof is omitted).
For every expression e, either e\to e' for some expression e' or e is a normal form.
I decided to read one paper or article every week. This week's topic is programming language semantics, refer to Graham Huttons's paper Programming language semantics: It's easy as 1,2,3.

Semantics is the general term for the study of meaning. Programming language semantics gives precise mathematical meaning to programs. We use a simple arithmetic expression language (including integers and addition only) to illustrate the basic concepts. This is an example of Occam's razor, a philosophical principle that favours the simplest explanation for a phenomenon.

Now let's define our language of arithmetic expressions built up from the set of integers and the operation of addition. Use a context-free grammar.
E:\equiv \mathbb {Z} | E+E

An expression is either an integer value or the addition of two sub-expressions. We assume that parentheses can be freely used as required to disambiguate expressions written in normal textual form. This grammar can be easily translated into a Haskell data type.

html:pre.html:code: data Expr = Val Integer | Add Expr Expr

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now we consider denotational semantics, where the terms in a language is defined using a valuation function that maps terms into values in an appropriate semantic domain.

Formally, for a language T of syntactic terms comprises two components: a set V of semantic values and a valuation function of type T\to V that maps terms to their meanings as values. This function is written by enclosing a term in a semantic brackets (Also known as Oxford or Strachey brackets), writing \llbracket t\rrbracket for the value of term t. In addition, the valuation function is required to be compositional, the meaning of a compound term is defined purely in terms of the meaning of its sub-terms.

Compositionality aids understanding by ensuring that the semantics is modular and supports the use of simple equational reasoning techniques for proving properties of the semantics. When the set of semantic values is clear, a denotational semantics is often identified with the underlying valuation function.

Given that terms and their semantics are built up inductively, proofs about denotational semantics typically proceed using structural induction. Let us show that our expression semantics is total, that is, for every expression e there is an integer n such that \llbracket e\rrbracket = n.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter: For the base case e = \text {Val} \space n, we have \llbracket e\rrbracket = n trivially. For the inductive case e = \text {Add} \space e_1\space e_2, we can assume by induction that \llbracket e_1\rrbracket = n_1 and \llbracket e_2\rrbracket = n_2 for some integers n_1 and n_2. Then \llbracket e\rrbracket = n_1 + n_2 by definition of the valuation function, indicates this case is also true. Therefore, the semantics is total.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The valuation function can be translated into a Haskell function

html:pre.html:code: eval :: Expr -> Integer eval (Val n) = n eval (Add x y) = eval x + eval y

fr:mainmatter.html:p: More generally, a denotational semantics can be viewed as an evaluator (or interpreter). Even eval is defined recursively, the semantics is compositional its behavior can be understood as simply replacing the constructors for expressions by other functions. In this manner, a denotational semantics can also be viewed as an evaluation function that is defined by folding over the syntax of the source language.

html:pre.html:code: eval :: Expr -> Integer eval = fold id (+)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The fold operator captures the ideas of replacing constructors of the language by other functions

html:pre.html:code: fold :: (Integer -> a) -> (a -> a -> a) -> Expr -> a fold f g (Val n) = f n fold f g (Add x y) = g (fold f g x) (fold f g y)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that the above semantics for expressions does not specify the order of evaluation. If we do wish to make evaluation order explicit this requires the introduction of additional structure into the semantics, named abstract machines (Discuss later).

Another popular approach to semantics is the operational approach, where the meaning of terms is defined using an execution relation that specifies how terms can be executed in an appropriate machine model. There are two basic forms of operational semantics:
small-step: describes the individual steps of execution
big-step: describes the overall results of execution
In this section we consider the small-step approach, which is also known as structural operational semantics.

Formally, a small-step operational semantics for a language T of syntactic terms comprises two components: a set S of execution states and a transition relation of type S\to S that specifies how terms can be executed. If there is a transition from state s to state s' in a single execution step, we write s\to s'.

The first rule states that two values can be added to give a single value and is called a reduction (or contraction) rule. An expression that matches such a rule is termed a reducible expression or redex. The last two rules are called structural (or congruence) rules as they specify how larger terms can be reduced.

The semantics is non-deterministic because an expression may have more than one possible transition. This is obviously from the structural rules, which allow either sub-expression to be reduced first.

Evaluation of an expression using the small-step semantics proceeds by a series of zero or more transition steps. Formally we can write e\to ^* e' to indicate that e can be reduced to e' in zero or more steps. We can generate a transition tree that captures all possible execution paths for an expression. Using the list comprehension we can define a function that returns the list of all expressions that can be reduced from a given expression e in a single transition.
