html:pre.html:code: trans :: Expr -> [Expr] trans (Val n) = [] trans (Add (Val n) (Val m)) = [Val (n + m)] trans (Add x y) = [Add x' y | x' <- trans x] ++ [Add x y' | y' <- trans y]

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define a Haskell datatype for transition trees and an execution function that converts expressions into transition trees.

html:pre.html:code: data Tree a = Node a [Tree a] exec :: Expr -> Tree Expr exec e = Node e [exec e' | e' <- trans e]

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Though exec is defined recursively, its behavior can be understood as simply applying the identity function to give the root of the tree and the transition function to generate a list of residual expressions to be processed to give the subtrees. A small-step semantics can be viewed as giving rise to an execution function that is defined by unfolding to transition trees.

html:pre.html:code: exec :: Expr -> Tree Expr exec = unfold id trans

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The unfold function captures the idea of generating a tree from a seed value x by applying a function f to give the root and a function g to give a list of residual values to be processed for the subtrees.

html:pre.html:code: unfold :: (t -> a) -> (t -> [t]) -> t -> Tree a unfold f g x = Node (f x) [unfold f g x' | x' <- g x]

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The operational semantics corresponds to unfolding to transition trees, while denotational semantics corresponds to folding over syntax trees. Thinking about semantics in terms of recursion operators reveals a duality

For denotational semantics we have structural induction, dual to this, for operational semantics we have rule induction. This allows us to perform proofs by considering the structure of the rules that are used to define the semantics.

The small-step semantics for expressions above has one basic reduction rule for adding values and two structural rules that allow addition to be performed in larger expressions. Separating these two kinds of rules results the notion of contextual semantics (or reduction semantics).

Informally, a context in this setting is a term with a "hole", usually written as [-], which can be filled with another term later. In a contextual semantics, the hole represents the location where a single basic step of execution may take place within a term.

Consider the following transition in our small-step semantics.
(1+2)+(3+4)\to 3+(3+4)
The addition is performed on the left side. We say that we can perform the basic step 1+2\to 3 in the context [-]+(3+4) where [-] implies the location of the addition takes place.

The language C of contexts of arithmetic expressions can be formally defined by
C:\equiv [-]|C+E|E+C
As previously, we can define a Haskell datatype for contexts.

html:pre.html:code: data Cont = Hole | Add Cont Expr | Add Expr Cont

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
The kind of context is known as "outside-in" as locating the hole involves navigating from the outside of the context inwards. To fill the hole in a context c with an expression e we write c\space [e]:
\begin {align*} \text {Hole}\space [e] &= e \\ (\text {AddL}\space c\space r)\space [e] &= \text {Add}\space (c\space [e])\space r \\ (\text {AddR}\space l\space c)\space [e] &= \text {Add}\space l\space (c\space [e]) \end {align*}

We have now refactored the small-step semantics into a single reduction rule and a single structural rule. If we subsequently want to extend the language with other features, it only requires adding new reduction rules and extending the notion of contexts but not need to adding new structural rules.
Now we define the hole filling function in Haskell.

html:pre.html:code: fill :: Cont -> Expr -> Expr fill Hole e = e fill (AddL c r) e = Add (fill c e) r fill (AddR l c) e = Add l (fill c e)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The dual operation which splits an expression into all possible pairs of contexts and expressions can be defined:

html:pre.html:code: split :: Expr -> [(Cont,Expr)] split e = (Hole, e) : case e of Val n -> [] Add l r -> [(AddL c r, x) | (c, x) <- split l] ++ [(AddR l c, x) | (c, x) <- split r]

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A pair (c,x) comprising a context #[c] and an expression x is an element of the list returned by split e precisely when fill c x = e. The contextual semantics can be translated into Haskell function that returns the lists of all expressions that can be reached by performing a single reduction step.

html:pre.html:code: reduce :: Expr -> [Expr] reduce (Add (Val n) (Val m)) = [Val (n + m)] reduce _ = []

fr:mainmatter.html:p: or a single transition step.

html:pre.html:code: trans :: Expr -> [Expr] trans e = [fill c x' | (c, x) <- split e, x' <- reduce x]

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This function splits the given expression into all possible context and expression pairs, then considering any reduction that can made by each component expression, and finally filling the hole in the context with the reduced expression.

Notice that the contextual semantics does not specify an evaluation order for addition and is non-deterministic. We can modify the language of contexts to achieve so.
C:\equiv [-]|C+E|\mathbb {Z}+C
This version of the semantics also satisfies a unique decomposition property, that is, any expression e that is not a value can be uniquely decomposed into the form e=c\space [x] for some context c and reducible expression x. This can be proved by induction on the expression e.
Contexts are related to a number of other important concepts in programming and semantics, including the use of continuations to make control flow explicit (John C. Reynolds 1972).

Big-step semantics is also known as natural semantics, which focus on large execution step. For a language T of syntactic terms comprises two components: a set V of values and an evaluation relation between T and V that relates each term to all values that can be reached by fully executing the term. If a term t and a value v are related, we say that t can evaluate to v and write this as t\Downarrow v
The Haskell function definition is similar to the small-step semantics, by using the list comprehension.

html:pre.html:code: eval :: Expr -> [Integer] eval (Val n) = [n] eval (Add x y) = [n + m | n <- eval x, m <- eval y]

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
This is similar to denotational semantics but using inference rules rather than a functional manner. However, there is no need for a big-step semantics to be compositional. Formally, the denotational and big-step semantics for the expression language are equivalent, which can be captured by the following property:
\llbracket e\rrbracket = n \iff e\Downarrow n
This is easily verified by induction.

All the examples we have encountered focused on explaining semantic ideas, now we show how language of integers and addition can also be used to help discover semantic ideas. We show how it can be used as the basis for discovering how to implement an abstract machine.
Remember the evaluation order problem we meet before, if we want to make evaluation order explicit, we can introduce additional structure into the semantics by constructing an abstract machine.

Formally, an abstract machine is usually defined by a set of syntactic rewrite rules that make explicit how each step of evaluation proceeds. This section we show how an abstract machine for our example language can be systematically derived from the evaluation function using steps based on two important semantic concepts, continuations and defunctionalisation.
We want to make the order of evaluation explicit in the semantics itself. A standard technique for achieving this aim is to rewrite the semantics in continuation-passing style.

In our setting, a continuation is a function that will be applied to the result of an evaluation. Formally, for our semantics eval :: Expr -> Integer, a continuation is a function of type Integer -> Integer that will be applied to the resulting integer to give a new integer. (This type can be generalized to Integer -> a, but we do not need now) We capture the notion of such a continuation using the following type declaration:

html:pre.html:code: type Continuation = Integer -> Integer

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We now define a new semantics \text {eval}', which takes an expression and returns an integer as previously but also takes a continuation as an additional argument, which is applied to the result of evaluating the expression.

html:pre.html:code: eval' :: Expr -> Continuation -> Integer

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The behavior of \text {eval}' should be:

We want to calculate a definition that satisfies the specification. Using structural induction on the expression e, we construct the term \text {eval}'\space e\space c by gradually removing the reference to eval. For the base case, e = \text {Val}\space n we have
For the inductive case, e = \text {Add}\space x\space y we begin in the same way:

However, no further definition can be applied now, so we consider the inductive hypothesis: Forall c' and c'' we have \text {eval}'\space x\space c' = c'(\text {eval}\space x) and \text {eval}'\space y\space c'' = c''(\text {eval}\space y). This can readily be achieved by abstracting over \text {eval}\space x and \text {eval}\space y using lambda abstraction.
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \begin {align*} & c\space (\text {eval}\space x + \text {eval}\space y) \\ =& (\lambda n\to c\space (n+\text {eval}\space y)) \\ =& \text {eval}'\space x\space (\lambda n\to c\space (n+\text {eval}\space y)) \\ =& \text {eval}'\space x\space (\lambda n\to (\lambda m\to c\space (n+m))(\text {eval}\space y)) \\ =& \text {eval}'\space x\space (\lambda n\to \text {eval}'\space y\space (\lambda m\to c\space (n+m))) \end {align*}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The final term does not refer to \text {eval} now. In summary we have calculated the following definition

html:pre.html:code: eval' :: Expr -> Continuation -> Integer eval' (Val n) c = c n eval' (Add x y) c = eval' x (\n -> eval' y (\m -> c (n + m)))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Our original semantics can be recovered from the new semantics by using the identity continuation \lambda n \to n

html:pre.html:code: eval e = eval' e (\n -> n)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We use continuation to make the order of evaluation explicit in the semantics, but this also makes the semantics into a higher-order function. Hence our second step is to regain the first-order nature of the original semantics by eliminating the use of continuations but retaining the explicit order of evaluation they introduced.

A standard technique for eliminating the use of functions as arguments is defunctionalisation. We do not usually need the entire function-space of possible argument functions, there only a few forms of such functions are actually used. Hence we represent the argument functions that we actually need using a datatype rather than functions.
We begin by defining three combinators halt, next and add for constructing the continuations we used.

html:pre.html:code:
halt :: Continuation halt n = n
next :: Expr -> Continuation -> Continuation next y c = \n -> eval' y (add n c)
add :: Integer -> Continuation -> Continuation add n c = \m -> c (n + m)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Use the combinators, our continuation semantics can now be written as:

html:pre.html:code:
eval :: Expr -> Integer eavl e = eval' e halt
eval' :: Expr -> Continuation -> Integer eval' (Val n) c = c n eval' (Add x y) c = eval' x (next y c)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now we declare a new datatype for continuations, consists of three constructors.

html:pre.html:code: data CONT = HALT | NEXT Expr CONT | ADD Integer CONT

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The following translation function forms a denotational semantics for CONT

html:pre.html:code: exec :: CONT -> Continuation exec HALT = halt exec (NEXT y c) = next y (exec c) exec (ADD n c) = add n (exec c)

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
This function is usually called apply, which can be viewed as applying a representation of a continuation to an integer to give another integer. We want to define a new semantics \text {eval}' which behaves in the same way as our previous \text {eval}' except that it uses values of type CONT rather than Continuation.
eval'' :: Expr -> CONT -> Integer
The desired behavior of \text {eval}'' is:
\text {eval}''\space e\space c = \text {eval}'\space e\space (\text {exec}\space c)

As before, we proceed by structural induction on expression e. The base case e=\text {Val}\space n is trivial
\begin {align*} \text {eval}''\space (\text {Val}\space n)\space c &= \text {eval}'\space (\text {Val}\space n)\space (\text {exec}\space c) \\ &= \text {exec}\space c\space n \\ \end {align*}

In the basic case, \text {exec} still refers to the semantic \text {eval}', via the combinator \text {next}. Hence we need to compute a new definition for \text {exec} that refers to our new \text {eval}''.
The other case is also easy to compute, no need to induction.
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \begin {align*} \text {exec}\space (\text {NEXT}\space y\space c)\space n &= \text {eval}''\space y\space (\text {ADD}\space n\space c) \\ \text {exec}\space (\text {ADD}\space n\space c)\space m &= \text {exec}\space c\space (n+m) \end {align*}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Our original semantics \text {eval} can be recovered from the new semantics \text {eval}'' too.
In summary, we have calculated the following definitions:

html:pre.html:code:
eval'' :: Expr -> CONT -> Integer eval'' (Val n) c = exec c n eval'' (Add x y) c = eval'' x (NEXT y c)
exec :: CONT -> Integer -> Integer exec HALT n = n exec (NEXT y c) n = eval'' y (ADD n c) exec (ADD n c) m = exec c (n + m)
eval :: Expr -> Integer eval e = eval'' e HALT

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The four components (\text {eval}'', \text {eval}, \text {exec} and CONT) forms an abstract machine.

CONT is the type of control stack which comprises instructions that determine how the machine should continue after evaluating the current expression. Sometimes it is called an "eval/continue" machine. The control stack can also be defined as a list of instructions.
type CONT = [INST] data INST = NEXT Expr | ADD Integer
\text {eval} evaluates an expression and give an integer by simply call the \text {eval}'' with empty control stack \text {HALT}.

\text {eval}'' evaluates an expression in the context of a control stack. If the expression is an integer, we execute the control stack using this integer as an argument. If the expression is an addition, we evaluate the first argument x and place the instruction \text {NEXT}\space y on the top of the control stack.

\text {exec} executes the control stack. If the control stack is empty, then just return the integer argument as the result. If the top instruction is \text {NEXT}\space y, we evaluate y and place the instruction \text {ADD}\space n to the stack top. If the top instruction is \text {ADD}\space n,evaluation of the two arguments of an addition is complete, and we execute the remaining control stack in the context of the sum of the resulting integers.
This is a collection of notes on categorical semantics for type theories. The notes are based on the paper by Jason Z.S. Hu and NLab.

Over the last few decades, many type systems are designed for different purposes: general program safety, security, and correctness. The categorical semantics is a collection of methods which define meanings of types and programs in category theory.

Category theory is a branch of mathematics studying an abstract kind of mappings, called morphisms, and their algebraic relations. Its generality serves as a common language for navigating connections between different concepts in different areas. We will first go over some basic concepts in category theory.
Formally, a definition in category theory consists of two parts: data and axioms. The most basic definition is the category

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
A category C consists
A collection of objects C_0 (\text {Ob}(C)).
A collection C_1 (\text {Mor}(C)) of morphisms (arrows).
For every morphism f there are an object s(f) (source, domain) and an object t(f) (target, codomain).
For every pair of morphisms f, g such that t(f) = s(g), there is a morphism g \circ f (composition) (Also written gf or f;g).
For every object x, there is a morphism \text {id}_x (or 1_x) called identity.
The following properties hold:
s(g \circ f) = s(f) and t(g \circ f) = t(g).
s(1_x) = x and t(1_x) = x.
Composition is associative: h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f when t(f) = s(g), and t(g) = s(h).
Composition satisfies the identity laws: f \circ \text {id}_x = f and \text {id}_y \circ f = f If the identity map and its axioms are omitted then one speaks of a semicategory.

fr:title.text: With a family of collections of morphisms
fr:title.html:strong: With a family of collections of morphisms

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
A category C consists
A collection of objects C_0 (\text {Ob}(C)).
For every pair of objects x, y, a collection C_1(x, y) (\hom _C(x,y)) of morphisms from x to y.
For each pair of morphisms f in C_1(x,y) and g in C_1(y,z), a morphism g \circ f in C_1(x,z). called their composition.
For each object x, a morphism \text {id}_x in C_1(x,x) called the identity on x.
The following properties hold:
Composition is associative: h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f for all f in C_1(x,y), g in C_1(y,z), and h in C_1(z,w).
Composition satisfies the identity laws: f \circ \text {id}_x = f and \text {id}_y \circ f = f for all f in C_1(x,y). Usually we write \text {Mor}(C) for the disjoint union \bigsqcup _{x,y \in C_0} C_1(x,y).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We only talk about collections here, which is vague, because we do not specify they are sets or classes. If both objects and morphisms fit in sets, we say the category is small. For a counterexample, the category of all sets is not small. However, all functions between sets can be contained in a set. In this case, the category is locally small. When morphisms between two objects fit in a set, we call the set hom-set.

Since category theory is constructed to study structures and a category is actually a structure, we can talk about the category of all small categories \mathbf {Cat}. Similar to morphisms, we can define functor between categories.

A functor F from a category C to a category D is a map sending each x\in C to an object F(x)\in D and each morphism f:x\to y in C to morphism F(f):F(x)\to F(y) in D, such that
Composition is preserved: F(g\circ f) = F(g)\circ F(f).
Identity is preserved: F(\text {id}_x) = \text {id}_{F(x)}.
We can push this idea further by considering functors as objects and natural transformations as morphisms.

Let C and D be categories, the functor category D^C (or [C,D]) is the category whose
objects are functors from C to D.
morphisms are natural transformations between functors.

Here we use a commutative diagram to represent a natural transformation. When a diagram commutes, morphisms composed by different paths with the same end points are equal. The following diagram represents the equality that G(f)\circ \alpha _x = \alpha _y\circ F(f).

Though the theory is already rich by only considering sets and categories, it would not be interesting enough. We want to know a little more about the category that we are working with. To achieve so, we can require some additional structures on the category. A common structure is the cartesian product.
With this definition, it is natural to ask what can serve as a nullary product. The concept is characterized by terminal objects.

When making math statements, we often encounter concepts that are dual to each other. In category theory, this phenomenon is captured by the concept of duality. Intuitively, duality offers us free dual theorem from the original one.
For a category \mathcal {C}, the opposite category \mathcal {C}^{op} has the same objects as \mathcal {C}, but the morphisms are reversed.
For example, the product in the opposite category, all universal properties corresponds to a dual concept.

One important principle in type theory is the Curry-Howard Isomorphism (Propositions as types). It depicts the connection between logic and types. A program can represent a logical argument, and operations in logic find meaningful correspondences in program execution. The principle was later extended with category theory due to Lambek. In his work, he showed a correspondence between STLC and Cartesian Closed Categories (CCC) and revealed the connection between types and categories. The correspondence is called the Curry-Howard-Lambek Isomorphism.

In general, there are two approaches to understand or design a type system: the syntactic view and semantic view.
The syntactic view focuses on the syntactic structure of types and programs. We study about subject reduction, cut elimination and etc, simply by manipulating the syntax. It is usually more direct and easier to understand as it is often conducted via induction on some syntactic structures. And it also suggest algorithms which can be implemented. The disadvantage is that it is limited and hard to proof some properties like normalization.
The semantic approaches are more powerful in general. They are based on mathematical models of type systems. In exchange of the strength and generality, it is usually harder to understand and heavyweight, requires more intuition of the concepts.

One classical semantic approach to logic is algebraic logic. A logical system is modeled by some algebraic theory. (often related to lattices and semi-lattices). Famous examples include Boolean algebras for classic propositional logic and Heyting algebras for intuitionistic counterpart. The algebraic logic is a powerful tool to study the properties of logical systems, but has a limitation that all operations are limited in one structured set.
An important result from categorical semantics could be monads. In Moggi's paper, he showed that monads can be used to model computational effects.
It requires an operation over functors named whiskering

Let F,G:C\to D and H,D\to E be functors and \eta :F\to G be a natural transformation whose coordinate at any object A of C is \eta _A, then whiskering H and \eta yields the natural transformation H\circ \eta :H\circ F\to H\circ G whose coordinate at A is H(\eta _A).

Categorical logic is a new approach to logic, due to Lawvere. He showed that logical constructs are fundamentally just adjoint functors. This allows us to capture many logical constructs by using only one categorical concept. Adjoint also provides a strong guarantee about the derived syntactic formulation.

Let \mathcal {C} and \mathcal {D} be categories and a pair of functors F:\mathcal {C}\to \mathcal {D} and G:\mathcal {D}\to \mathcal {C}. This is called pair of adjoint functors (or adjunction) with F the left adjoint and G the right adjoint denoted
F\dashv G
if there is a natural isomorphism between the hom-functors:
\hom _{\mathcal {D}}(F(-),-)\cong \hom _{\mathcal {C}}(-,G(-))
which means forall objects C\in \mathcal {C} and D\in \mathcal {D}, there is a bijection
\hom _{\mathcal {D}}(F(C),D)\cong \hom _{\mathcal {C}}(C,G(D)) \\ (F(C)\xrightarrow {f}D) \mapsto (C\xrightarrow {G(f)}G(D))
which is natural in both C and D.

This post focus on the the algebra of graphs introduced in paper Algebraic graphs with class (functional pearl), which built on rigorous mathematical foundation that allows us to apply equational reasoning for proving the correctness of graph transformation algorithms.

Graphs are ubiquitous in computing. Roughly speaking, a graph is a collection of vertices and edges, where each edge connects two vertices. For the most trivial case, a graph is an ordered pair G=(V,E) comprising:
V is a set of vertices.
E \subseteq \{ (x,y) \mid x, y \in V\} is a set of edges. We can define a graph type in some programming languages (e.g. Haskell) as:
data Graph a = Graph [a] [(a, a)]
Work with such low-level fiddling with sets of vertices and edges is very painful. And we can easily construct a graph that breaks the invariant of the graph structure like Graph [1] [(1,2)] which has an edge connecting a non-existent vertex.

How the state-of-art libraries deal with this problem? The container library in Haskell provides a type Data.Graph which represents graph using adjacency array:
type Graph a = Array a [a]
which ensures performance and generality. But the consistency invariant is not statically checked, which may lead to runtime errors like index out of ranges. Another approach is the fgl (Martin Erwig's Functional Graph Library) where the graph is introduced as an inductive type. The approach is very complex and its API contains partial functions. So is there a safe graph construction interface we can build on top?

Andrey Mokhov's paper presents a new interface for constructing and transforming graphs in a safe and convenient manner. And abstract away from the actual representation details and characterize graphs by a set of axioms, just like numbers are algebraically characterized by rings. The core calculus is based on the algebra of parameterized graphs. Algebraic graphs have a safe and minimalistic core of four graph construction primitives, as captured by the following data type:
data Graph a = Empty | Vertex a | Overlay (Graph a) (Graph a) | Connect (Graph a) (Graph a)

The Empty and Vertex construct the empty and single-vertex graphs respectively. Overlay composes two graphs by taking the union of their vertices and edges, and Connect is similar to Overlay but also creates edges between vertices of the two graphs.
The overlay and connect operations have three properties:
(Closure) They are closed on the set of graphs (all total functions)
(Complete) They can be used to construct any graph starting from the empty and single-vertex graphs
(Sound) Malformed graphs are impossible to construct

The simplest possible graph is the empty graph. We denote it by \epsilon = (\varnothing , \varnothing ) . A graph with a single vertex is \text {Vertex} x = (\{x\}, \varnothing ) . To construct larger graphs from the above primitives we define binary operations overlay and connect, denoted by + and \to respectively. The overlay operation + is defined as:
(V_1, E_1) + (V_2, E_2) = (V_1 \cup V_2, E_1 \cup E_2)
The connect operation \to is defined similarly (We give it a higher precedence than + ):
(V_1, E_1) \to (V_2, E_2) = (V_1 \cup V_2, E_1 \cup E_2 \cup V_1 \times V_2)

As shown above, the core can be represented by a simple data type Graph, parameterized by the type of vertices a. We can push this further by defining a type class GraphLike that captures the core operations of the algebraic graph.

We abstract the graph construction primitives defined above as the type class Graph (Note that associated types requires TypeFamilies GHC extension):
class Graph g where type Vertex g empty :: g vertex :: Vertex g -> g overlay :: g -> g -> g connect :: g -> g -> g

This interface is very simple and easy to use, which allows fewer opportunities for usage errors and greater opportunities for reuse. Now let's create some functions to construct graphs. For instance, a single edge is obtained by connecting two vertices:
edge :: (Graph g) => Vertex g -> Vertex g -> g edge x y = connect (vertex x) (vertex y)

A graph that contains a given list of isolated vertices can be constructed as follows:
vertices :: Graph g => [Vertex g] -> g vertices = foldr (overlay . vertex) empty
which turns each vertex into a singleton graph and overlay the results. By replacing the overlay with connect we can construct a full connected graph.
clique :: (Graph g) => [Vertex g] -> g clique = foldr (connect . vertex) empty

The graph construction functions defined above are total, fully polymorphic, and elegant. Thanks to the minimalistic core type class, it is easy to wrap our favourite graph library into the described interface, and reuse the functions defined with graph class.

In this section we characterise the Graph type class with a set of axioms that reveal an algebraic structure very similar to a semiring. This provides a convenient framework for proving graph properties, using equational reasoning. The presented characterization is generally useful for formal verification, as well as automated testing of graph library APIs.

Notice that the clique and vertices functions use \epsilon as the identity element for the overlay and connect operation respectively. Further more we can verify:
(G,+,\epsilon ) is an idempotent commutative monoid.
(G,\to ,\epsilon ) is a monoid.
\to distributes over +. This looks like a semiring, but the identity element are shared between the two operations. What makes the algebra of graphs different is the decomposition law:
x \to y \to z = x \to y + x \to z + y \to z
Interestingly, the fact that overlay and connect share the same identity follows from the decomposition law. Furthermore, the identity (x + \epsilon = x) and idempotence (x + x = x) can also be proved from the decomposition law. Hence we get a minimal set (8) of axioms that characterize the algebraic graphs.
+ is commutative and associative: x + y = y + x and (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)
(G,\to ,\epsilon ) is a monoid, i.e. x \to y \to z = x \to (y \to z) and \epsilon \to x = x, x \to \epsilon = x
\to distributes over +: (x + y) \to z = x \to z + y \to z
Decomposition law: x \to y \to z = x \to y + x \to z + y \to z By adding more axioms we can obtain more complex graphs such as directed graphs, hypergraphs, etc.

Algebraic graphs are complete in the sense that it is possible to describe any graph using the core interface. Indeed, given a graph G=(V , E) we can construct it as graph V E, where the function graph is defined as follows.
graph :: (Graph g) => [Vertex g] -> [(Vertex g, Vertex g)] -> g graph vs es = overlay (vertices vs) (edges es)
where edges is defined as:
edges :: (Graph g) => [(Vertex g, Vertex g)] -> g edges = foldr (overlay . uncurry edge) empty
The absorption theorem x \to y + x + y = x \to y, derived from decomposition of x \to y \to \epsilon , states that an edge (u, v) contains its two vertices u, v and is inseparable from them. Therefore, if the pair (V , E) is inconsistent, the set of vertices V will be expanded to \hat {V} so that E\subseteq \hat {V} \times \hat {V} holds. More generally, the absorption theorem states that in addition to being complete, the algebraic graph API is also sound in the sense that it is impossible to construct an inconsistent pair (V , E) using the four Graph methods.

There are many other interesting properties of algebraic graphs can be proved using the axioms:
(Overlay Identity) x + \epsilon = x
(Overlay Idempotence) x + x = x
(Absorption) x \to y + x + y = x \to y
(Saturation) x \to x \to x = x \to x

It is fairly standard to define x \leq y as x + y = y for an idempotent operation +, since it gives a partial order on the elements of the algebra. Formally we call this definition the subgraph relation. Therefore, we can check if a graph is a subgraph of another one if we know how to compare graphs for equality.
isSubgraphOf :: (Graph g, Eq g) => g -> g -> Bool isSubgraphOf x y = overlay x y == y
Now we define some instances of the Graph, and extend the axioms to construct more complex graphs.

We start by a direct encoding of the graph construction primitives defined into the abstract data type Relation isomorphic to a pair of sets (V , E):
data Relation a = R {domain :: Set a, relation :: Set (a, a)} deriving (Eq)
instance (Ord a) => Graph (Relation a) where type Vertex (Relation a) = a empty = R Set.empty Set.empty vertex x = R (singleton x) Set.empty overlay x y = R (domain x `union` domain y) (relation x `union` relation y) connect x y = R (domain x `union` domain y) ( relation x `union` relation y `union` fromAscList [(a, b) | a <- elems (domain x), b <- elems (domain y)] )
As we have seen, this implementation satisfies the axioms of the graph algebra. Furthermore, it is a free graph in the sense that it does not satisfy any other laws. This follows from the fact that any algebraic graph expression g can be rewritten in the following canonical form:
g = \left ( \sum _{v\in V_g} v \right ) + \left ( \sum _{(u,v)\in E_g} u \to v \right )
The existence of the canonical form was proved by Mokhov in Algebra of Parameterised Graphs for an extended version of the algebra. The core idea is to repeatedly apply the decomposition law to rewrite the graph expression in the form of the above equation, until no further decomposition is possible.

It will be convenient to make Relation an instance of Num type class.
instance (Ord a, Num a) => Num (Relation a) where fromInteger = vertex . fromInteger (+) = overlay (*) = connect signum = const empty abs = id negate = id
With these setups we can use the standard + and \times operators as shortcuts for overlay and connect respectively. Note that the Num law abs x * signum x == x is satisfied by the above definition since x \to \epsilon = x. Any Graph instance can be made an instance of Num if needed.
Notes about algebraic effects and handlers.
In algebra we study mathematical structures that are equipped with operations satisfying equational laws.

A signature \Sigma is a collection of operation symbols with arities \{(\text {op}_i, \text {ar}_i)\}_i. The operation symbols opi may be any anything, but are usually thought of as syntactic entities, while arities \text {ar}_i are non-negative integers. An operation symbol whose arity is 0 is called a constant or a nullary symbol. Operation symbols with arities 1, 2 and 3 are referred to as unary, binary, and ternary, respectively.

A list of distinct variables x_1, \cdots , c_k is called a context. The \Sigma \text {-terms} in this context are built inductively using the following rules:
Each variable x_i is a \Sigma \text {-term} in this context
If t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i} are \Sigma \text {-terms} in this context, then \text {op}_i(t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i}) is a \Sigma \text {-term} in this context We write
x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid t
to indicate that t is a \Sigma \text {-term} in the context x_1, \cdots , x_k. A closed \Sigma \text {-term} is a term in the empty context.

A \Sigma \text {-equation} is a pair of \Sigma \text {-terms} l and r in the context x_1, \cdots , x_k:
x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid l = r
We shall often elide the context and write simply l = r.
An algebraic (equational) theory T = (\Sigma _T, E_T) is given by a signature \Sigma _T and a collection \Epsilon _T of equations over the terms of this signature.

Let \Sigma be a signature, an interpretation I of \Sigma is given by the following data:
A set |I| called the carrier of the interpretation
For each operation symbol \text {op}_i, a map
[\text {op}_i]_I : |I|^i \to |I|
The bracket []_I here is called the semantic bracket and is typically used when syntactic entities (operation symbols, terms, equations) are mapped to their mathematical counterparts.

The interpretation can be extended to terms and equations. A \Sigma \text {-term} t in the context x_1, \cdots , x_k is interpreted as a function
[x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid t]_I : |I|^k \to |I|
as follows:
The variable x_i is interpreted as the i-th projection
[x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid x_i]_I : |I|^k \to |I|, \quad (a_1, \cdots , a_k) \mapsto a_i
A compound term in context x_1, \cdots , x_k is interpreted as the composition of the semantic brackets of the operation symbols and the terms:
|I|^k \xrightarrow {[t_1]_I, \cdots , [t_{\text {ar}_i}]_I} |I|^{\text {ar}_i} \xrightarrow {[\text {op}_i]_I} |I|

A model M of an algebraic theory T is an interpretation of the signature \Sigma _T which validates all the equations E_T. That is, for each equations x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid l = r in E_T, we have:
[x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid l]_M = [x_1, \cdots , x_k \mid r]_M
We refer to a model of T as a T\text {-algebra} or T\text {-model}.

Let M and N be models of an algebraic theory T. A T-homomorphism from M to N is a function f:|M|\to |N| that preserves the interpretation of the operations of T. That is, for each operation symbol f\in \Sigma _T, we have:
f_N \circ (f, \cdots , f) = f \circ f_M
where f_M and f_N are the interpretations of f in M and N respectively. We say that f is a model isomorphism if it is bijective. We say that M and N are isomorphic if there exists a model isomorphism between them.
We may organize the models of an algebraic theory T into a category \mathbf {Mod}(T) whose objects are the models of the theory and the morphisms are the model homomorphisms.

So far we have considered the models of an algebraic theory as sets with operations. More generally we can consider models in any category C with finite products. Hence the definition of an interpretation and a model may be directly transcribed.

An interpretation I in C is given by
An object |I| in C, called the carrier
For each operation symbol \text {op}_i, a morphism in C
[\text {op}_i]_I : |I|^i \to |I|
Notice that a nullary symbol is interpreted as a morphism |I|^0 \to |I|, which is a morphism form the terminal object 1\to |I| in C.

Similarly, the interpretation can be extended to terms and equations in the same way. A model of an algebraic theory T in C is an interpretation M of its signature \Sigma _T which validates all the equations E_T. The definition of a homomorphism is now the morphism in the category C. The T\text {-models} and T\text {-homomorphisms} in C form another category, denoted by \mathbf {Mod}_C(T).
Of special interest are the free models of an algebraic theory.

Let T be an algebraic theory and X be a set, the free T-model, also called the free T-algebra, generated by X is a model M together with a map \eta :X\to |M| such that for any T-model L and every map f:X\to |L|, there is a unique T-homomorphism \bar {f}:|M|\to |L| such that the following diagram commutes:
This can be understood as follows: the free T-model generated by X is the most economical way of making a T-model out of the set X. ("Free" essentially means with as few assumptions as possible.)

For instance, the free group generated by the singleton set \{a\} is the infinite cyclic group, which is isomorphic to \mathbb {Z}. If you have an element a, then you automatically have all its powers of a in the group. We can not make any further assumptions because we need to send this free group to any other group that satisfies the group axioms, the powers of a are going to be "interpreted".

Every algebraic theory T has a free model. Given a signature \Sigma and a set X, define \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X) to be the set of well-founded trees built inductively as follows:
\forall x \in X, there is a tree \text {return}(x) \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X) (the choice of the label is immaterial in fact)
For each operation symbol \text {op}_i and trees t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i} \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X), there is a tree, denoted by \text {op}_i(t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i}) \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X), whose root is labeled by \text {op}_i and whose children are subtrees t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i}.
In this setting, the \Sigma \text {-terms} in the context x_1, \cdots , x_k are the trees in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (\{x_1, \cdots , x_k\}). A variable x_i is labeled as \text {return}(x_i) when construed as a tree. Suppose x_1, \cdots , x_n \mid t is a term in context and we are given an assignment \sigma : \{x_1, \cdots , x_n\} \to \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X). We can build the tree \sigma (t) inductively as follows:
\sigma (t) = \sigma (x_i) if t = x_i
\sigma (t) = \text {op}_i(\sigma (t_1), \cdots , \sigma (t_{\text {ar}_i})) if t = \text {op}_i(t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i}) Briefly, the tree \sigma (t) is obtained by replacing each variable x_i in t with the corresponding tree \sigma (x_i).

Let \sim _T be the least equivalence relation on \text {Tree}_{\Sigma _T}(X) such that:
For every equation x_1, \cdots , x_n \mid l = r in E_T and for every assignment \sigma we have: \sigma (l) \sim _T \sigma (r)
\sim _T is a congruence: for every operation symbol \text {op}_i in \sigma _T and forall trees s_1,\cdot ,s_{\text {ar}_i} and t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i} in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X), if
s_1 \sim _T t_1 \quad \cdots \quad s_{\text {ar}_i} \sim _T t_{\text {ar}_i}
then the following holds:
\text {op}_i(s_1, \cdots , s_{\text {ar}_i}) \sim _T \text {op}_i(t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i})

Now we define the carrier the free model F_T(X) to be the quotient set
|F_T(X)| = \text {Tree}_{\Sigma _T}(X)/\sim _T
Let \langle t \rangle be the \sim _T equivalence class of t \in \text {Tree}_{\Sigma _T}(X), the interpretation of the operation symbol \text {op}_i in the free model is defined by:
[\text {op}_i]_{F_T(X)}(\langle t_1 \rangle , \cdots , \langle t_{\text {ar}_i} \rangle ) = \langle \text {op}_i(t_1, \cdots , t_{\text {ar}_i}) \rangle
and the map \eta _X : X \to F_T(X) is defined by
\eta _X(x) = \langle \text {return}(x) \rangle
Note that if theory T has no equations, the free models generated by T is the set of all trees in \text {Tree}_{\Sigma _T}(X) because the equivalence relation \sim _T is the identity relation =.
So far we have developed the algebraic theories, to get a better fit with computational effects, we need to generalize operations in two ways: arities and parameters.

Generalizing arities: One might expect that the generalization of arities is to allow them to be ordinal or cardinal numbers, hence they can fit the infinity. However, that would be a non-computational idea. Instead, we can generalize the arities to be functions. Notice that the n-ary cartesian product of X is isomorphic to the exponential X^{[n]}, where [n] = \{1, \cdots , n\}. Now we replace [n] with arbitrary set A, then we can think of a map X^A \to X as arguments of arity A. We need a reasonable notation for writing down an operation symbol to A\text {-many} arguments, where A is an arbitrary set. To achieve this, we introduce the map \kappa :A\to X, and thus we simply write \text {op}_i(\kappa ) for the operation symbol.
Generalizing parameters: We can generalize operations to take parameters from a set P, this naturally models algebraic operations that arise as computational effects.

Compose them together: Now we can restate the definitions of signatures and algebraic operations with the generalizations incorporated. https://caimeo.space/def-004T/def-004T/def-004T/Parameterized Operations and General AritiesDefinition
A signature \Sigma is given by a collection of operation symbols \text {op}_i with associated parameters sets P_i and arity A_i, denoted \text {op}_i: P_i \rightsquigarrow A_i.
The terms in context are generalized to well-founded trees over \Sigma generated by a set X. These form a set \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X) whose elements are inductively generated:
for every x \in X, there is a tree \text {return}(x) \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X)
If p \in P_i and \kappa : A_i \to \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X), then there is a tree \text {op}_i(p, \kappa ) \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X), whose root is labeled by \text {op}_i and subtrees are given by the trees in the image of \kappa .
The elements of \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X) may be thought of as \Sigma \text {-terms} with variables X.
An interpretation I of a signature \Sigma is given by (here we assume that the category is a category of sets, the more general cases are omitted for brevity):
A set |I| called the carrier of the interpretation
For each operation symbol \text {op}_i: P_i \rightsquigarrow A_i, a map
[\text {op}_i]_I : P_i \times |I|^{A_i} \to |I|
The interpretation can be extended to terms (trees). A tree t \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X) is interpreted as a map
[t]_I : |I| ^ X \to |I|
as follows:
The tree \text {return}(x) is interpreted as the projection map:
[\text {return}(x)]_I : \eta \mapsto \eta (x)
A compound tree is interpreted as the composition of the semantic brackets of the operation symbols and the subtrees:
[\text {op}_i(p, \kappa )]_I : \eta \to [\text {op}_i]_I(p, \lambda a. [\kappa (a)]_I(\eta ))
A \Sigma \text {-equation} is a set X and a pair of trees l, r \in \text {Tree}_\Sigma (X):
X\mid l = r
Given an interpretation I of signature \Sigma , we say that such an equation is valid for I if l and r are interpreted as the same map. The algebraic theory, models and categories are generalized similarly, we do not repeat here.

fr:title.text: Vector Calculus and Geometry of Space

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Vector Calculus and Geometry of Space

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes about multi-variable calculus, geometry of space and linear algebra. Refer to A Visual Introduction to Differential Forms and Calculus on Manifolds.
We now start with introducing the vector space over the field of real numbers \mathbb {R}.

A vector space over a field F is a non-empty set V together with a binary operation and a binary function that satisfy the axioms listed below. In this context, the elements of V are commonly called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars.
Commutativity: \forall x, y \in V, x + y = y + x
Associativity: \forall x, y, z \in V, (x + y) + z = x + (y + z)
Additive Identity: \exists 0 \in V \text { such that } \forall x \in V, x + 0 = x
Multiplicative Identity: \forall x \in V, 1x = x
Additive Inverse: \forall x \in V, \exists y \in V \text { such that } x + y = 0
Distributivity: \forall x, y \in V, \forall c, d \in F, c(x + y) = cx + cy, (c + d)x = cx + dx
Elements of a vector space are called vectors or points.

Now we will consider a certain type of transformation between vector spaces called a linear transformation. Suppose T is a mapping between \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m, that is T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m, then T is a linear transformation if:
T(c \cdot \vec {v}) = c \cdot T(\vec {v}) \\ T(\vec {v} + \vec {w}) = T(\vec {v}) + T(\vec {w})
If T is a linear transformation from \mathbb {R}^m to \mathbb {R} we simply call it a linear function or a linear functional.

We now turn our attention to the relationship between linear transformation and matrices. We just stick to vector spaces \mathbb {R}^n and the standard basis made up of the Euclidian unit vectors. In order to write linear transformation T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m as a matrix we need ordered bases for both \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m. We can use the intuitively obvious order e_1 < e_2 < \cdots < e_n. Now we can give formal definition of the matrix representation of a linear transformation.

fr:title.text: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation over \R ^n

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation over \R ^n

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Suppose that T:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m is a linear transformation between vector spaces \mathbb {R}^n and \mathbb {R}^m. Let e_1, e_2, \ldots , e_n be the standard basis of \mathbb {R}^n and f_1, f_2, \ldots , f_m be the standard basis of \mathbb {R}^m. Then the matrix representation of T is the m \times n matrix A such that for 1\leq j\leq n:
T(e_j) = \sum _{i=1}^m A_{ij} f_i
where the matrix representation of T is given by the m\times n matrix with entries A_{ij}.

The last major topic in this section is the definition of the dual space. In our discussion, we only concern the dual space of \mathbb {R}^n which is denoted as (\mathbb {R}^n)^*. Now let's consider the dual basis of (\mathbb {R}^n)^* which is denoted as \{T_1, \cdots , T_n\}, which is defined by:
T_i(e_j) = e^i(e_j) = \langle e^i, e_j \rangle = \delta _{j}^i
where \delta _{ij} is the Kronecker delta. We say that T_i is dual to the vector e_i. Note that we also denote T_i as e^i using superscript notation. And the notation \langle e^i, e_j \rangle d indicates the products of row vector e^i and column vector e_j (Usually used in quantum computing).
\alpha (v) = \langle \alpha , v \rangle = [a,b] \times \begin {bmatrix} x \\ y \end {bmatrix} = ax + by
This explains what we always denote elements of the vector space as column vectors, because elements of the dual space are written as row vectors and its very important to distinguish between them.

In linear algebra, dot product or scalar product is an operation that takes two vectors and returns a scalar. Geometrically, it is the product of the Euclidean magnitudes of the two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them. Dot product is also used to define lengths and angles.

The dot product of two vectors \vec {a} = (a_1, a_2, \cdots , a_n) and \vec {b} = (b_1, b_2, \cdots , b_n) is defined as
\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + \cdots + a_nb_n = \sum _{i=1}^n a_ib_i.
The dot product is also called the inner product or scalar product. The dot product satisfies the following properties:
Commutative: \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = \vec {b}\cdot \vec {a}
Distributive: \vec {a}\cdot (\vec {b} + \vec {c}) = \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} + \vec {a}\cdot \vec {c}
Bilinear: \vec {a}\cdot (k\vec {b}) = k(\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b}) = (\vec {a}\cdot k\vec {b})
Scalar Multiplication: (c_1\vec {a}) \cdot (c_2\vec {b}) = c_1c_2(\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b})
Orthogonality: If \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = 0, then \vec {a} and \vec {b} are orthogonal
Product Rule: If \vec {a} and \vec {b} are vector valued differentiable functions then the derivative of \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} is given by the rule (\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b})' = \vec {a}'\cdot \vec {b} + \vec {a}\cdot \vec {b}'

In Euclidean space, a Euclidean vector is a geometric object that possesses both a norm and a direction. The dot product of two vectors \vec {a} and \vec {b} is defined as
\vec {a}\cdot \vec {b} = \lVert \vec {a}\rVert \lVert \vec {b}\rVert \cos \theta
where \theta is the angle between the two vectors.

Two points determine a line, and so does a point and a vector. Define the base point vector \vec {b}=(x,y,z) and the direction vector \vec {v}=(a,b,c) then the line is given by \vec {r}(t)
\vec {r}(t) = t\vec {v} + \vec {b} = (at+x, bt+y, ct+z)
Solving for t in the equation we get
t = \frac {x-at}{a} = \frac {y-bt}{b} = \frac {z-ct}{c}
which is the equation of line.

The determinant has various properties and applications in linear algebra and geometry. For us the most useful thing about it will be how it relates to volume: the determinant of a matrix gives the signed volume of the parallelepiped that is generated by the vectors given by the matrix columns.

Determinants can be introduced in a variety of different ways but many of them are not at all clear. It usually relates to volume hence we will actually use our intuitive understanding of volumes and three properties that we expected volume to have to derive the determinant (It is uniquely determined!).

So how do we expect volume to behave? First we expect a unit cube to have a volume of one. Second we expect the degenerate parallelepiped to have a volume of zero. Basically in n dimensions any n-1 dimensions object has zero n-D volume. Third we expect that volumes to be linear. Now with these three properties we move to the actual mathematics.

Suppose we have a parallelepiped \mathscr {P}\in \mathbb {R}^n whose edges are given by v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n\in \mathbb {R}^n. We sat that the parallelepiped \mathscr {P} is the span of the vectors v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n and write \mathscr {P}=\text {span}\{v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n\} (Note that this span is different from linear span). We want to find function D:\mathbb {R}^{n\times n}\to \mathbb {R} which takes v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n or a matrix with v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n as columns to a real number which is the volume of \mathscr {P}. Now we present the three properties in mathematical form.

html:ul.html:li: D(I) = I where I = [e_1, e_2, \cdots , e_n] is the identity matrix.
D(v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n) = 0 if v_i = v_j for any i\neq j.

D(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, v+cw, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) \\ = D(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, v, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) + cD(v_1, \cdots , v_{j-1}, w, v_{j+1}, \cdots , v_n) for any 1 \leq j \leq n, that is, D is linear.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now we use these properties of volume to derive several other useful properties. The first property is that the volumes are signed.

html:ul.html:li:
D is alternating, if we switch any two vectors the sign changes.
D(v_1, \cdots , v_i, \cdots , v_j, \cdots , v_n) = -D(v_1, \cdots , v_j, \cdots , v_i, \cdots , v_n)

If v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n are linear dependent then
D(v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n) = 0
Adding a multiple of one vector to another does not change the determinant.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We almost ready to derive the formula for determinant. The final ingredient we need to do is permutations.

A permutation of a set S is a bijection from S to itself. The set of permutation of \{1,\cdots , n\} is usually denoted by S_n. We often denote a particular permutation \sigma by Cauchy's two-line notation:
\begin {bmatrix} 1 & 2 & \cdots & n \\ \sigma (1) & \sigma (2) & \cdots & \sigma (n) \end {bmatrix}
or Cauchy's one-line notation: (\sigma (1),\sigma (2),\cdots ,\sigma (n)). Another common notation is the cycle notation:
(i_1\ i_2\ \cdots \ i_k) which means i_1 \to i_2 \to \cdots \to i_k \to i_1.
A permutation in which only two elements are exchanged is called a transposition. The notation is \tau _{i,j} where i and j are the two elements exchanged while the others remain fixed.

Notice that the composition of two permutations is also a permutation. And for any permutation \sigma we can perform a series of transpositions to get the identity permutation. It turns out that the count of the number of transpositions needed to get the identity permutation is always the same, which is called the parity of the permutation.

The sign of a permutation \sigma \in S_n is a function \text {sgn}:S_n\to \{-1,1\} defined as \text {sgn}(\sigma ) = 1 if \sigma requires an even number of permutations and \text {sgn}(\sigma ) = -1 if \sigma requires an odd number of permutations to get the identity permutation.

It's easy to validate that the following properties of the determinant holds:
D(AB) = D(A)D(B)
D(A) = D(A^T) The second statement for transpose of A indicates that all the properties above also holds for row as well.

Since f'(x_0) represents the slope of the line tangent to the graph of f at (x_0, f(x_0)), differentiability of f at x_0 means that there exists a number m st
\lim _{x\to x_0} \frac {|f(x) - f(x_0) - m(x-x_0)|}{|x-x_0|} = 0
Now consider the function T:\mathbb {R}\to \mathbb {R} where T(s) = ms
T(s+t) = m(s+t) = ms + mt = T(s) + T(t) \\ T(cs) = mcs = c(ms) = cT(s)
then T is a linear transformation. In fact T is the linear function that most closely approximates the function f at the point (x_0, f(x_0)). So for x values that are very close to x_0 we have
f(x) \approx m(x-x_0) + f(x_0)

Now let's generalize the concept of derivatives to functions of the form f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m. We assume the function f has the form
\begin {align*} &f(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n) = \\ &(f_1(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n), f_2(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n), \cdots , f_m(x_1, x_2, \cdots , x_n)) \end {align*}
We want to search for this linear transformation which we will denoted by Df, that most closely approximates this function f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m at some specific point x_0=(x_{1_0}, x_{2_0}, \cdots , x_{n_0}) \in \mathbb {R}^n. If f is differentiable at x_0 then there exists a linear transformation Df(x_0):\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R}^m such that
\lim _{x\to x_0} \frac { \lVert f(x) - f(x_0) - Df(x_0)(x-x_0) \rVert }{\lVert x-x_0\rVert } = 0
The \lVert \cdot \rVert represents the Euclidean norm of the vector (Multi-dimensional version of the absolute value)
\lVert \vec {x}\rVert = \sqrt {x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2} = \sqrt {\sum _{i=1}^n x_i^2}
which is just the length of the vector. This allows us to perform dividing.
This post shows operations and applications over matrix, refers to Wikipedia.

The transpose of a matrix A, denoted by A^T is the matrix obtained by swapping the rows and columns of A. It satisfies the following properties:
(A^T)^T = A
(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T
(cA)^T = cA^T
(AB)^T = B^TA^T

If the following condition satisfies:
a_{ij} = a_{ji} \quad \forall i,j
Then the matrix is called symmetric.

A square matrix A is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:
A = A^T
This also implies A^{-1} A^T = I

The determinant of a n\times n square matrix A is commonly denoted \det A or |A|. It satisfies the following properties:
\det A^T = \det A
\det AB = \det A \det B
\det \lambda A = \lambda ^n \det A
To compute the inverse of a matrix, we need Adjugate matrix.

If A is a square matrix, then the minor of the entry in the i-th row and j-th column (also called the (i, j) minor, or a first minor) is the determinant of the sub-matrix formed by deleting the i-th row and j-th column. The (i, j) minor is denoted as M_{ij}. The Cofactor is obtained by multiplying the minor by (-1)^{i+j}.

The matrix formed by all of the cofactors of a square matrix A is called the cofactor matrix, or comatrix:
C = \left [ \begin {array}{cccc} C_{11} & C_{12} & \cdots & C_{1n} \\ C_{21} & C_{22} & \cdots & C_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ C_{n1} & C_{n2} & \cdots & C_{nn} \end {array} \right ]
The Adjugate matrix of A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

Then the inverse of A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix times the reciprocal of the determinant of A:
A^{-1} = \frac {1}{\det A} \cdot \text {adj} A = \frac {1}{\det A} \cdot C^T
A square matrix that is not invertible is called singular or degenerate

fr:title.text: An important property of the inverse of a matrix

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An important property of the inverse of a matrix

html:p.fr:tex: A \cdot \text {adj} A = \text {adj} A \cdot A = \det A \cdot I

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let A \cdot \text {adj} A = (b_{ij}) and we have
b_{ij} = a_{i1}A_{j1} + a_{i2}A_{j2} + \cdots + a_{in}A_{jn} = \delta _{ij} \cdot \det A
Hence we have A \cdot \text {adj} A = \det A \cdot I

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
A matrix polynomial is a polynomial with square matrices as variables. The general form of a matrix polynomial is:
P(A) = \sum _{i=0}^{n} a_i A^i
where A^0 = I is the identity matrix.

If A is a diagonal matrix, then the polynomial of A is the diagonal matrix of the polynomial of the diagonal elements of A.
p(A) = \begin {bmatrix} p(a_{11}) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & p(a_{22}) & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & p(a_{nn}) \end {bmatrix}

If A = P\Lambda P^{-1}, then A^k = P \Lambda ^k P^{-1} and hence
p(A) = a_0 I + a_1 A + a_2 A^2 + \cdots + a_n A^n = P \Lambda P^{-1}

Consider a system of n linear equations for n unknowns, represented in matrix multiplication form as follows:
A \cdot X = B
where A is a square matrix of order n, X is a column matrix of order n and B is a column matrix of order n.
X = \begin {bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end {bmatrix}
The Cramer's rule states that the solution to the system of equations is given by:
x_i = \frac {\text {det}(A_i)}{\text {det}(A)}
where A_i is the matrix obtained by replacing the ith column of A by B.
Matrix partitioning is the process of dividing a matrix into smaller submatrices. This is often done to simplify the computation of matrix operations, such as matrix multiplication.

There are three types of elementary matrices, which correspond to three types of row operations (respectively, column operations, row operations are equivalent to multiplying on the left by the corresponding elementary matrix, and column operations are equivalent to multiplying on the right by the corresponding elementary matrix):
Row switching: A row within the matrix can be switched with another row.
P_{i,j} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & 0 & & 1 \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & 1 & & 0 \\ & & & & & \ddots \\ & & & & & & 1 \end {bmatrix}
Row multiplication: Each element in a row can be multiplied by a non-zero constant.
D_i(k) = \text {diag} (1, \cdots , k, \cdots , 1)
Row additio: A row can be replaced by the sum of that row and a multiple of another row.
T_{i,j} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 \\ & \ddots \\ & & 1 & & k \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & & & 1 \\ & & & & & \ddots \\ & & & & & & 1 \end {bmatrix}

Two matrices A,B are column / row equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of elementary operations, denoted A \sim B. The column / row equivalence is an equivalence relation.

We can show that a matrix A is invertible iff there are finite elementary matrices E_1, E_2, \cdots , E_n such that
A = E_1E_2\cdots E_n

From above we can deduce that a square matrix A is invertible iff A\sim E. This trick can be used for solving a linear system and computing the inverse of a matrix. For instance, given AX=B we can solve X by the following steps: Let P be a matrix such that PA=I where I is the identity matrix. Hence P = A^{-1} and we have X = PB, we can do elementary operations over matrix (A, B) to get the solution of X.
Now let's talk about the concept of rank. In linear algebra, the (column)rank of a matrix A is the dimension of the vector space generated (or spanned) by its columns.

The rank of a linear map or operator \Phi is defined as the dimension of its range:
\text {rank}(M)\equiv \dim (\text {range }(M))
Note that the range (column space) of a matrix M is the span of its column vectors.

Similarly we can define the row rank of a matrix. A fundamental result in linear algebra is that the column rank and the row rank are always equal. Hence we can simply call it the rank of a matrix. If the column rank equals to the column size, we say that the matrix is full column rank.

A common approach to finding the rank of a matrix is to reduce it to a simpler form, generally row echelon form, by elementary row operations. Row operations do not change the row space (hence do not change the row rank), and, being invertible, map the column space to an isomorphic space (hence do not change the column rank).
A \sim B \implies \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(B) \\ \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(A^T)
Once in row echelon form, the rank is clearly the same for both row rank and column rank, and equals to the number of pivots (or basic columns) and also the number of non-zero rows.

A matrix is in row echelon form if
All rows having only zero entries are at the bottom
The leading entry (that is, the left-most nonzero entry) of every nonzero row, called the pivot, is on the right of the leading entry of every row above.
Some texts add the condition that the leading coefficient must be 1 while others require this only in reduced row echelon form.

The determinantal rank of a matrix is the order of the largest non-zero minor of the matrix. It is also the number of non-zero eigenvalues of the matrix. This does not give an efficient way of computing the rank, but it is useful theoretically: a single non-zero minor witnesses a lower bound for the rank of the matrix, which can be useful to prove that certain operations do not lower the rank of a matrix.

We can conclude the properties of rank:
\begin {align*} &0 \leq \text {rank}(A_{m\times n}) \leq \min (m,n) \\ &\text {rank}(A^T) = \text {rank}(A) \\ & A \sim B \implies \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(B) \\ & P, Q \text { is invertible} \implies \text {rank}(PAQ) = \text {rank}(A) \\ & \max (\text {rank}(A), \text {rank}(B)) \leq \text {rank}(A, B) \leq \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \\ & \text {rank}(A+B) \leq \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \\ & \text {rank}(AB) \leq \min (\text {rank}(A), \text {rank}(B)) \\ & A_{m\times n}B_{n\times l} = O\implies \text {rank}(A) + \text {rank}(B) \leq n \end {align*}

With such properties we can prove an important theorem:
AB = O \land A \text { is full rank} \implies B = O
which is known as the cancellation law of matrix multiplication.

The rank of a matrix is also related to the solution of a linear system. If the rank of the coefficient matrix is less than the rank of the augmented matrix, then the system is inconsistent. Hence there does not exist a solution. Similarly we have the following discussion: For a n-variable linear system Ax = b
If \text {rank}(A) < \text {rank}(A,b), the solution does not exist.
If \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(A,b)=n, there is a unique solution.
If \text {rank}(A)=\text {rank}(A,b)<n, there are infinite solutions.
This leads two fundamental theorems of linear systems:
n-variable regular linear system Ax = 0 has a non-trivial solution iff \text {rank}(A) < n.
Matrix equation AX = B has solutions iff \text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(A,B).

Let V be a vector space over a field F. Let v_1, \dots , v_n be vectors in V. A linear combination of v_1, \dots , v_n is an expression of the form
a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n
where a_1, \dots , a_n \in F.

Given two sets of vectors, we say that they are equal iff their elements can write as linear combinations of each other. This condition can be written using rank:
\text {rank}(A) = \text {rank}(B) = \text {rank}(A, B)

A set of vectors \{v_1, \dots , v_n\} is called linearly independent if a_1 v_1 + \dots + a_n v_n = 0 implies that a_1 = \dots = a_n = 0. The trivial case of \{0\} is also considered linearly independent.
Notes about the classic mechanics. Most of the content is based on the Wikipedia page about the subject.

The motion of a body can only be described relative to something else—other bodies, observers, or a set of spacetime coordinates. These are called frames of reference. All physical laws take their simplest form in an inertial frame. Galilean invariance or Galilean relativity states that the laws of motion are the same in all inertial frames of reference.

An increase in the kinetic energy of a rigid body is caused by an equal amount of positive work done on the body by the resultant force acting on that body. Conversely, a decrease in kinetic energy is caused by an equal amount of negative work done by the resultant force.

Work on a free (no fields), rigid (no internal degrees of freedom) body, is equal to the change in kinetic energy E_k corresponding to the linear velocity and angular velocity of that body.
W = \Delta E_k

The work of forces generated by a potential function is known as potential energy and the forces are said to be conservative. Work on an object that is merely displaced in a conservative force field, without change in velocity or rotation, is equal to minus the change of potential energy E_p of the object
W = -\Delta E_p

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The work done in accelerating a particle with mass m during the infinitesimal time interval dt is given by the dot product of force \vec {F} and the infinitesimal displacement d\vec {x}
dW = \vec {F} \cdot d\vec {x} = \frac {d\vec {p}}{dt} \cdot \vec {v}dt = \vec {v}\cdot d\vec {p} = \vec {v} \cdot d(m\vec {v})
Applying the product rule of differentiation, we get:
d(\vec {v}\cdot \vec {v}) = 2\vec {v} \cdot d\vec {v}
Therefore we have:
\vec {v} \cdot d(m\vec {v}) = \frac {m}{2} d(\vec {v} \cdot \vec {v})
Since this is a total differential (that is, it only depends on the final state, not how the particle got there), we can integrate it and call the result kinetic energy:
E_k = \int _{v_1}^{v_2} \vec {p} \cdot d\vec {v} = \frac {1}{2} m (v_2^2-v_1^2)

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
If a rigid body Q is rotating about any line through the center of mass then it has rotational kinetic energy (E_r) which is simply the sum of the kinetic energies of its moving parts, and is thus given by:
E_r = \int _Q \frac {v^2dm}{2} = \int _Q \frac {(r\omega )^2dm}{2} = \frac {\omega ^2}{2}\int _Qr^2dm = \frac {1}{2}I\omega ^2
I = \int _Qr^2dm is the moment of inertia of the body.
\omega is the angular velocity of the body.
r is the distance from the axis of rotation.

Momentum depends on the frame of reference, but in any inertial frame it is a conserved quantity, meaning that if a closed system is not affected by external forces, its total linear momentum does not change.

For a system with one or more particles, the total momentum is the sum of the momenta of the individual particles.
\vec {p} = \sum m_i \vec {v}_i
Or use the center of mass:
\vec {p} = M \vec {V}
where M is the total mass of the system and \vec {V} is the velocity of the center of mass. This formula is known as the Euler's first law of motion.
In a closed system the total momentum remains constant. A closed system means that the system is not affected by external forces. Or approximately the external forces are extremely small.
The above statement leads to the Conservation of Angular Momentum.

When a body is free to rotate around an axis, torque must be applied to change its angular momentum. The amount of torque needed to cause any given angular acceleration is proportional to the moment of inertia of the body. The moment of inertia plays the role in rotational kinetics that mass (inertia) plays in linear kinetics, both characterize the resistance of a body to changes in its motion.
The SHM note is based on Wikipedia.

In mechanics and physics, simple harmonic motion is a special type of periodic motion an object experiences by means of a restoring force whose magnitude is directly proportional to the distance of the object from an equilibrium position and acts towards the equilibrium position.

In Newtonian mechanics, for one-dimensional simple harmonic motion, the equation of motion, which is a second-order linear ordinary differential equation with constant coefficients, can be obtaind by Hooke's law and Newton's second law.
F_{\mathrm {net} }=m{\frac {\mathrm {d} ^{2}x}{\mathrm {d} t^{2}}}=-kx,
where m is the inertial mass og the oscillating body, x is its displacement from the equilibrium position and k is a constant. Therefore we have
{\frac {\mathrm {d} ^{2}x}{\mathrm {d} t^{2}}}=-{\frac {k}{m}}x,
solving the differential equation we get the sinusoidal function
x(t)=C_{1}\cos \left (\omega t\right )+C_{2}\sin \left (\omega t\right ),
where \omega =\sqrt {\frac {k}{m}}.

Let t=0 we see that C_1 = x(0) so that C_1 is the initial position. Taking the derivative of the equation and evaluating at 0 we get x'(0) = \omega C_2. So C_2 is the initial speed of the object diverged by the angular frequency, C_2 = \frac {v_0}{\omega }. Thus
x(t)=x_{0}\cos \left ({\sqrt {\frac {k}{m}}}t\right )+{\frac {v_{0}}{\sqrt {\frac {k}{m}}}}\sin \left ({\sqrt {\frac {k}{m}}}t\right ).

This equation can also be written in the form:
x(t) = Acos(\omega t-\phi )
where
\begin {align*} A = \sqrt {C_{1}^{2}+C_{2}^{2}} \\ \phi = \arctan \left (\frac {C_{2}}{C_{1}}\right ) \\ \sin \phi = \frac {C_{2}}{A} \\ \cos \phi = \frac {C_{1}}{A} \end {align*}
Each of these constants carries a physical meaning of the motion: A is the amplitude and \omega = 2\pi f is the angular frequency and \phi is the initial phase.

The kinetic energy of the object at time t is given by
K(t)={\tfrac {1}{2}}mv^{2}(t)={\tfrac {1}{2}}m\omega ^{2}A^{2}\sin ^{2}(\omega t-\varphi )={\tfrac {1}{2}}kA^{2}\sin ^{2}(\omega t-\varphi )
Besides the kinetic energy, the potential energy of the object at time t is given by
U(t)={\tfrac {1}{2}}kx^{2}(t)={\tfrac {1}{2}}kA^{2}\cos ^{2}(\omega t-\varphi )
The total energy of the object is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies
E=K+U={\tfrac {1}{2}}kA^{2}
which is a constant value. Notice that if we solve v from the energy equation we get
v = \pm \sqrt {\frac {k}{m}(A^{2}-x^{2})} = \pm \omega \sqrt {A^{2}-x^{2}}
which implies that the velocity is maximum when the displacement is zero and vice versa.

According to the principle of superposition of SHM, the resultant displacement of a number of waves in a medium at a particular point is the vector sum of the individual displacements produced by each of the waves at that point. Consider two waves having the same angular frequency (Suppose \phi _2 > \phi _1) in the same line:
x_{1}(t)=A_{1}\cos (\omega t+\phi _{1}) \\ x_{2}(t)=A_{2}\cos (\omega t+\phi _{2})
Use vector addition we can easily compute the resultant displacement
A = \sqrt {A_{1}^{2}+A_{2}^{2}+2A_{1}A_{2}\cos (\phi _{2}-\phi _{1})} \\
and the resultant initial phase
\phi = \arctan \left (\frac {A_{1}\sin \phi _{1}+A_{2}\sin \phi _{2}}{A_{1}\cos \phi _{1}+A_{2}\cos \phi _{2}}\right )

For some special case, the resultant displacement can be simplified:
If \phi _2 - \phi _1 = 2k\pi , k \in \mathbb {Z} then the resultant displacement is
A = A_{1}+A_{2}
If \phi _2 - \phi _1 = (2k+1)\pi , k \in \mathbb {Z} then the resultant displacement is
A = |A_{1}-A_{2}|

If two waves are perpendicular to each other
x = A\cos (\omega t + \alpha ) \\ y = B\cos (\omega t + \beta )
we can compute that
\frac {x^2}{A^2} + \frac {y^2}{B^2} - \frac {xy}{AB}\cos (\beta -\alpha ) = \sin ^2(\beta -\alpha )
which is the equation of an ellipse.

html:ul.html:li:
\beta - \alpha = 0 \text { or } \pi the ellipse becomes two line:
(\frac {x}{A}\pm \frac {y}{B})^2 = 0 \implies y = \pm \frac {B}{A}x
The trajectory is two straight line cross the origin. The resultant amplitude is C = A^2 + B^2

\beta - \alpha = \pm \frac {\pi }{2} the ellipse becomes a regular ellipse, i.e., the ellipse that takes the coordinates axis as its major axis.
\frac {x^2}{A^2} + \frac {y^2}{B^2} = 1
If \beta - \alpha > 0 the ellipse is clockwise, otherwise it is counter-clockwise.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A wave is a propagating dynamic disturbance (change from equilibrium) of one or more quantities. Waves are often described by a wave equation (standing wave field of two opposite waves) or a one-way wave equation for single wave propagation in a defined direction.

There are two types of waves that are commonly stdudied: mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.
A mechanical wave is a local deformation (strain) in some physical medium that propagates form particle to particle by creating local stresses that cause strain in neighboring particles.
The electromagnetic wave us propagating by the coupling between the electric and magnetic fields. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum and through some dielectric media.
According to the direction of vibration and propagation, waves can be classified into two types.

html:ul.html:li: A transverse wave is a wave that oscillates perpendicularly to the direction of the wave's advance.
A longitudinal wave is a wave that oscillates parallel to the direction of the wave's advance.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The wavelength, frequency, speed and period are four import quantities of a wave. Now we give their relations.
The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the displacements of the individual waves at that point.
The Huygens principle states that each point on a wavefront is a source of spherical wavelets and the wavefront at a later time is the envelope of these wavelets.

If the displacement of origin O can be expressed as
y_O = A\cos (\omega t)
Such a vibration propagates along x-axis, the displacement of a point P (at x) at time t is
y = A\cos (\omega t - 2\pi f \frac {x}{v}) = A\cos \omega (t - \frac {x}{v})
The distance between P and O is x, in this time period the origin vibrates \frac {x}{v}f times. Every vibration changes the phase with 2\pi . Hence P is behind O in 2\pi f \frac {x}{v} in phase.

When constructing a semantic model of a system or when structuring computer code, there are several notions of computation that one might consider. The popular ones can be monads, applicative functors and arrows. Each of these notions of computation has particular characteristics that makes them more suitable for some tasks than for others. In fact, these representations can be unified as monoids in a monodial category, and there is much to be gained from unifying all three different notions under a single conceptual framework.
Monads are known to be monoids in a monoidal category of endofunctors
Arrows have been recently shown to be strong monoids in a monoidal category of profunctors
Applicative functors are usually presented as lax monoidal functors with a compatible strength, or monoids in a monoidal category of endofunctors using the Day convolution as a tensor
For every set M we can construct the monoid of endomorphisms (M\to M, \circ , \text {id}).

M is a sub-monoid of a monoid M' if there is an injection i : M \hookrightarrow M' such that i(e) = e' and i(a \circ b) = i(a) \circ ' i(b) for all a, b \in M. Every monoid M is a sub-monoid of the monoid of endomorphisms (M\to M, \circ , \text {id}).

This can be proved by constructing an injection map \text {rep} : M\to (M\to M) by \text {rep} : a \mapsto \lambda x.a\circ x, which is easy to verify that \text {rep} is a monoid homomorphism. Moreover, \text {rep} is an injection, since we have a function \text {abs} : (M\to M) \to M given by \text {abs} : f \mapsto f(e). and \text {abs}\circ \text {rep} = \text {id}_M.
The Cayley representation can be adapted to the List ([a], ++, []) in Haskell, resulting the famous Difference Lists.

html:pre.html:code:
type EList a = [a] -> [a]
rep :: [a] -> EList a rep xs = (xs ++)
abs :: EList a -> [a] abs f = f []

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
The ordinary notion of monoid in category Set of sets and functions is restrictive, so generalize monoids to other categories. What we need are notions of
a pairing operation for expressing the type of the multiplication,
a type for expressing the unit.
We can not directly extend set binary functions X \times X \to X to monoid multiplication in a category, because the category may not have products. Instead, we need to use a bifunctor \otimes : C \times C \to C which abstracts the product operation. The unit object is a special object I in the category.
The idea of currying a function can be generalized to a monoidal category with exponential.

Let A be an object of a monoidal category (C, \otimes , \alpha , \lambda , \rho ). An exponential -^A is the right adjoint to the functor - \otimes A, which is characterised by the an isomorphism:
\lfloor -\rfloor : \hom (X \otimes A, B) \cong \hom (X, B^A) : \lceil - \rceil
natural in X and B. The counit of the adjunction is the evaluation map \ev _B : B^A \otimes A \to B. When the exponential to A exists, we say A is an exponent. A monoidal category with all exponentials is called a right-closed monoidal category or said to have exponentials.
For a set A we can generate the free monoid A^*. We can then define the notion of free monoid in terms of monoidal category.

Monoids in a monoidal category C and monoid homomorphisms form a category, denoted by \text {Mon}(C). When the left-adjoint (-)^* to the forgetful functor U : \text {Mon(C)} \to C exists, it maps an object X to the free monoid on X.

It is well known that the free monoid over a set A is the set of lists of A. In Haskell this is just the list type List a.
data List a = Nil | Cons a (List a)
Given a monoid (M, e, m) in C, and a monic i : M' \hookrightarrow M in PC such that for some unique maps e' and m', the following diagram commutes:

fr:resource.fr:resource-source: \begin {tikzcd} && { M} && {M\otimes M} \\ I \\ && {M'} && {M' \otimes M'} \arrow ["m"', from=1-5, to=1-3] \arrow ["e", from=2-1, to=1-3] \arrow ["{e'}", from=2-1, to=3-3] \arrow ["i", from=3-3, to=1-3] \arrow ["{i \otimes i}"', from=3-5, to=1-5] \arrow ["{m'}"', from=3-5, to=3-3] \end {tikzcd}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then (M', e', m') is a sub-monoid of (M, e, m), induced by the monic i, which is a monoid monomorphism from M' to M.
Every exponent in a monoidal category induces a monoid of endomorphisms.

Let (C, \otimes , I, \alpha , \lambda , \rho ) be a monoidal category. The monoid of endomorphisms on any exponent A \in C is given by the diagram:
I \xrightarrow {i_A} A^A \xleftarrow {c_A} A^A \otimes A^A
where i_A and c_A are defined:
\begin {align*} i_A &= \lfloor I \otimes A \xrightarrow {\lambda _A} A \rfloor \\ c_A &= \lfloor (A^A \otimes A^A)\otimes A \xrightarrow {\alpha ^{-1}} A^A\otimes (A^A \otimes A) \xrightarrow {\text {id}_{A^A} \otimes \text {ev}_A} A^A\otimes A \xrightarrow {\text {ev}_A} A \rfloor \end {align*}
The Cayley theorem states that every monoid in a monoidal category is a sub-monoid of endomorphisms whenever M is an exponent.

Let \text {End} = ([\text {Set}, \text {Set}], \circ , \text {Id}, \alpha , \lambda , \rho ) be a (strict, i.e. \alpha ,\lambda ,\rho are identities) monoidal category of endofunctors. A monoid in this category consists of
an endofunctor M : \text {Set} \to \text {Set}
a natural transformation \mu : M \circ M \to M
a unit e : \text {Id} \to M such that the following diagrams commute:

fr:resource.fr:resource-source: \begin {tikzcd} {(M \circ M)\circ M} &&&& {M\circ M} \\ \\ {M\circ (M\circ M)} && {M\circ M} && M \arrow ["mM"', from=1-1, to=1-5] \arrow [equal, from=1-1, to=3-1] \arrow ["m", from=1-5, to=3-5] \arrow ["Mm"', from=3-1, to=3-3] \arrow ["m"', from=3-3, to=3-5] \end {tikzcd}

\begin {tikzcd} {M\circ M} && {M\circ \text {Id}} \\ \\ {\text {Id}\circ M} && M \arrow ["m", from=1-1, to=3-3] \arrow ["Me", from=1-3, to=1-1] \arrow [equal, from=1-3, to=3-3] \arrow ["eM", from=3-1, to=1-1] \arrow [equal, from=3-1, to=3-3] \end {tikzcd}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A monoid in \text {End} is called a monad. That is where the slogan "a monad is a monoid in the category of endofunctors" comes from.
The monad can be implemented as the type class Triple in Haskell.

html:pre.html:code: class Functor m => Triple m where unit :: a -> m a join :: m (m a) -> m a

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The familiar implementation is the Kleisli extension one: (Note that one can be obtained from the other by taking unit = return and join = (>>= id), (>>= f) = join . fmap f)

html:pre.html:code: class Monad m where return :: a -> m a (>>=) :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b
